articles.title: Lula diz que PL decidiu apoiar fim da escala 6x1 'depois da pressão da sociedade' | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente afirmou que manifestações nas ruas pressionaram o partido; nesta terça, Flávio Bolsonaro declarou voto favorável à PEC após ter criticado a proposta.
articles.summary: Presidente afirmou que manifestações nas ruas pressionaram o partido; nesta terça, Flávio Bolsonaro declarou voto favorável à PEC após ter criticado a proposta.
articles.body:
Lula durante cerimônia nesta terça (13) no Palácio do Planalto. — Foto: Reprodução/Lula

O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva afirmou nesta terça-feira (13) que o PL decidiu apoiar o fim da escala de trabalho 6x1 após pressão da sociedade e manifestações nas ruas.

“Me parece que, depois da pressão da sociedade, me parece que depois de todas as manifestações na rua deste Brasil, o partido do PL resolveu votar o fim da escala 6x1”, disse Lula .

Nesta terça, o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), adversário de Lula no segundo turno da eleição presidencial, declarou que votará a favor da PEC ( veja vídeo abaixo ).

Até então crítico da proposta, Flávio afirmou que decidiu se posicionar “conforme a vontade da maioria do povo”.

Depois de mencionar a mudança de posição, Lula fez uma provocação à direita.

“Eu, de vez em quando, fico pensando: se todo mal que eu causar a esse país for fazer a direita avançar e atender aos interesses do povo brasileiro, eu vou continuar fazendo isso”, afirmou.

As declarações do presidente foram dadas nesta manhã durante cerimônia no Palácio do Planalto que anunciou medidas para microempreendedores individuais .

Nos últimos dias, Lula vinha cobrando publicamente uma posição de Flávio e do PL sobre o tema.

Na quinta (8), o presidente afirmou que partido e candidato não queriam assumir o compromisso de aprovar a PEC.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsorano (PL) — Foto: Reprodução/Ricardo Stuckert/Vittor Sales

O texto reduz a jornada máxima de 44 para 40 horas semanais e garante dois dias de descanso remunerado por semana, sem redução salarial.

O Senado deve votar a proposta em primeiro turno nesta quarta (14) . Para ser aprovada, a PEC precisa de pelo menos 49 dos 81 votos e ainda terá de passar por um segundo turno.

Nas últimas semanas, governistas têm tentado acelerar a tramitação , enquanto aliados de Flávio Bolsonaro buscaram adiar a votação.

articles.title: Bloqueio de celulares em presídios: Governo publica novo decreto | G1
articles.standfirst: Em busca da reeleição, o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) tem mobilizado o discurso em torno da pauta da segurança pública.
articles.summary: Bloqueio de celulares em presídios será agilizado por novo decreto federal para combater o crime organizado e reforçar a segurança pública no país.
articles.body:
Às vésperas do segundo turno, o governo federal publicou um decreto nesta terça-feira (13) que cria um programa nacional para agilizar o bloqueio de celulares e de outros meios de comunicação utilizados ilegalmente dentro de presídios.

Em busca da reeleição, o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) tem mobilizado o discurso em torno da pauta da segurança pública, uma das principais preocupações dos eleitores e um tema que costuma mobilizar o debate nacional.

Na última semana, Lula afirmou que o lema de sua campanha agora é: 'Para o povo trabalhador, proteção; para o bandido, prisão' , e defendeu a aprovação da Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC), que prevê uma maior participação do governo federal no combate ao crime organizado.

Quase 10 mil celulares foram apreendidos dentro de presídios de todo o país ao longo dos últimos três anos, durante operações de varredura em celas coordenadas pelo Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública.

O objetivo é retirar a capacidade de comunicação dos detentos. De posse desses aparelhos, os presidiários seguem praticando crimes de dentro das cadeias e conseguem falar com comparsas do lado de fora.

Pessoa digitando no celular - imagem de arquivo — Foto: Reprodução/TV Gazeta

O decreto do governo estabelece um mecanismo de cooperação entre União, estados, Distrito Federal e Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel).

A iniciativa prevê duas principais formas de atuação: o bloqueio de aparelhos celulares identificados individualmente e a interrupção de sinais de radiocomunicação dentro de perímetros de segurança delimitados ao redor das unidades prisionais.

Pelo modelo previsto, as administrações penitenciárias estaduais serão responsáveis por identificar as ocorrências e encaminhar informações técnicas para viabilizar o bloqueio.

A Anatel ficará responsável por adotar as medidas cabíveis dentro de suas competências legais, inclusive no caso de pedidos relacionados à operação de bloqueadores de sinais.

As informações serão encaminhadas por uma plataforma digital do Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública, integrada ao Sistema Nacional de Informações Penais (Sisdepen).

No caso de celulares individualizados, o pedido será direcionado ao fluxo de bloqueio do Banco Nacional de Celulares com Restrição. Já as solicitações relacionadas ao bloqueio de sinais em áreas delimitadas serão encaminhadas à Anatel.

articles.title: Flávio passa a declarar voto a favor da PEC fim da escala 6x1 | G1
articles.standfirst: Flávio vinha sendo cobrado por Lula por uma posição sobre a PEC apresentada por parlamentares de esquerda. Candidato do PL à Presidência vinha defendendo um modelo de negociação de jornada entre patrão e empregado.
articles.summary: Após cobranças de Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro declara voto favorável à PEC fim da escala 6x1 para atender ao desejo da maioria dos trabalhadores brasileiros.
articles.body:
Crítico da Proposta de Emenda à Constituição que acaba com a escala de trabalho 6x1 , o senador e candidato do PL à Presidência, Flávio Bolsonaro , passou a declarar nesta terça-feira (13) voto a favor da PEC sobre o tema em discussão no Senado .

A proposta, apresentada por parlamentares de esquerda, está na pauta do Senado e deve ser votada, em primeiro turno, nesta quarta-feira (14).

Flávio deu a declaração após visitar o pai, o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro , que cumpre, em regime domiciliar, pena de prisão por tentativa de golpe de Estado.

O candidato do PL ao Palácio do Planalto – que estava sendo cobrado pelo adversário na corrida presidencial, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ), a se manifestar sobre o tema – disse que se posicionará "conforme a vontade da maioria do povo".

"Eu estou rodando o Brasil. A maioria dos trabalhadores quer o fim da 6x1. Vou votar a favor do fim da 6x1, mas a gente defende algo ainda melhor, sempre", declarou Flávio em entrevista após visitar o pai.

Segundo Flávio, a ideia que ele defende é a de liberdade de negociação entre empregador e empregado, com "liberdade para a pessoa montar seus horários de trabalho".

"Como que fica a pessoa que trabalha de home office? Isso não está definido na PEC. Como é que fica aquela mãe que não tem com quem deixar o seu filho, só pode trabalhar por exemplo quatro horas por dia, só pode trabalhar de manhã, ou só pode trabalhar de tarde? Vai continuar engessada a jornada dela", declarou o candidato do PL.

🔎Apesar da fala do candidato do PL, a Consolidação das Leis do Trabalho ( CLT ) prevê regras para o teletrabalho ("home office") e para a trabalhadora gestante e para a puérpera, que deu à luz recentemente.

Na semana passada, ao comentar a proposta, Flávio afirmou que tinha um projeto "infinitamente melhor". "É dar liberdade ao trabalhador, que escolha a sua própria carga horária, trabalhar, por exemplo, 4 horas por dia, 4 horas de manhã ou 4 horas à tarde, ou trabalhar no final de semana. Nossa proposta é dar liberdade", afirmou o presidenciável do PL na ocasião.

Já o coordenador da campanha de Flávio, senador Rogério Marinho (PL-RN), disse, na semana passada, que a discussão sobre a PEC do fim da 6x1 neste momento "não faz bem para o país" . O parlamentar articulava o adiamento da análise. Marinho é o autor da proposta classificada por Flávio como "melhor" do que a PEC em discussão no Congresso.

Embora tenha feito críticas à PEC do fim da escala 6x1 na semana passada, Flávio disse nesta terça que a discussão sobre a jornada é um "processo de evolução". "A gente tem que fazer com que o trabalhador tenha direito a uma folga maior sim", declarou.

Nesta terça-feira, Flávio Bolsonaro se encontrou com o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, que cumpre em casa pena de 27 anos e 3 meses pela trama golpista.

Flávio estava desde julho deste ano sem poder visitar o pai, após o descumprimento de medidas cautelares impostas pelo Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) com a divulgação de uma carta de Jair em apoio à sua candidatura.

Nesta segunda-feira (12), após 90 dias de suspensão, o ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do STF, atendeu a um pedido da defesa do ex-presidente e autorizou a retomada das visitas de Flávio.

O candidato à presidência do Brasil, Flávio Bolsonaro, do Partido Liberal (PL), conversa com jornalistas após visitar seu pai, o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, que cumpre pena em prisão domiciliar, antes do segundo turno das eleições, em Brasília, Brasil, em 13 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: Diego Herculano/Reuters

articles.title: MDB vai anunciar apoio majoritário a Flávio Bolsonaro após ato nesta terça, diz presidente do partido | G1
articles.standfirst: Anúncio será feito durante o ato marcado para esta tarde, em São Paulo. Na ocasião, 17 dos 27 diretórios estaduais do partido deverão divulgar adesão à candidatura.
articles.summary: Anúncio será feito durante o ato marcado para esta tarde, em São Paulo. Na ocasião, 17 dos 27 diretórios estaduais do partido deverão divulgar adesão à candidatura.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro com o prefeito de São Paulo, Ricardo Nunes (MDB) e o governador reeleito do estado, Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos) — Foto: Vittor Sales

O presidente nacional do MDB, deputado federal Baleia Rossi (SP), afirmou nesta terça-feira (13) que o partido vai formalizar apoio majoritário à candidatura do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) à Presidência da República.

O anúncio será feito durante o ato marcado para esta tarde, em São Paulo. Na ocasião, 17 dos 27 diretórios estaduais do partido deverão divulgar adesão à candidatura.

Segundo Baleia Rossi, o apoio reúne diretórios de todas as regiões do país, inclusive do Nordeste . No primeiro turno, o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), candidato à reeleição, teve mais votos do que Flávio na região.

“Tomamos a decisão que o povo tomou nas urnas no primeiro turno, que é o desejo de mudança. E desejando que Flávio repita a gestão [de] Ricardo Nunes e [de] Tarcísio de Freitas”, afirmou o presidente do partido.

Ricardo Nunes, prefeito de São Paulo, é filiado ao MDB. Já o vice-governador paulista, Felicio Ramuth, é do mesmo partido.

Dos 27 diretórios estaduais do MDB, nove já haviam declarado apoio a Lula ainda no primeiro turno. Outros 17 devem oficializar a adesão a Flávio Bolsonaro, enquanto um diretório permanece neutro.

De acordo com Baleia Rossi, o posicionamento dos diretórios está consolidado. O presidente da legenda não espera mudanças de posição entre os grupos que apoiam os dois candidatos.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro faz primeira visita ao ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro após fim de restrições do STF | G1
articles.standfirst: Relator do caso, Moraes autorizou a retomada das visitas na segunda-feira (12). A restrição às visitas havia sido determinada após Flávio ler uma carta do pai, desrespeitando medidas judiciais decretadas pelo Supremo.
articles.summary: Relator do caso, Moraes autorizou a retomada das visitas na segunda-feira (12). A restrição às visitas havia sido determinada após Flávio ler uma carta do pai, desrespeitando medidas judiciais decretadas pelo Supremo.
articles.body:
O senador e candidato à Presidência Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) chegou à residência do pai, Jair Bolsonaro (PL), na manhã desta terça-feira (13) para fazer a sua primeira visita ao ex-presidente desde o fim das restrições determinadas pelo Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ).

Condenado a 27 anos e 3 meses de prisão por tramar um golpe de Estado, Jair Bolsonaro cumpre a pena na sua casa, no Jardim Botânico, em Brasília. Flávio chegou ao local por volta de 9h40, e saiu uma hora depois.

"Hoje visitei meu pai, Jair Bolsonaro. Saio muito feliz aqui, ele estava muito alegre com o resultado dessas eleições, o resultado do primeiro turno", afirmou Flávio à imprensa na saída.

"Agora, eu falando como filho fico muito feliz de poder dar um abraço no meu pai, olhar no olho dele e ver que ele está bem", prosseguiu.

Nesse domingo (12), o ministro Alexandre de Moraes autorizou a retomada das visitas do senador ao ex-presidente.

A decisão atendeu a um pedido da defesa de Jair Bolsonaro apresentado no dia 5 de outubro, e ocorre após o fim do período de 90 dias de suspensão imposto em julho, que terminou no sábado (11).

A proibição de visitas havia sido aplicada após Flávio usar uma visita para pegar uma carta do ex-presidente e divulgá-la nas redes sociais, descumprindo medidas cautelares impostas contra Jair Bolsonaro, que está preso em regime domiciliar por tentativa de golpe.

Flávio Bolsonaro diz que visitará o pai na terça-feira — Foto: Globo/ Reprodução

A carta divulgada por Flávio, em julho, continha uma manifestação do ex-presidente em apoio a candidatura do filho.

Apesar de liberar o retorno das visitas, que devem seguir os mesmos horários e regras estabelecidos antes da suspensão, o ministro manteve a proibição de finalidade político-eleitoral e a divulgação de quaisquer manifestos ou declarações do ex-presidente, inclusive por terceiros.

Na decisão, Moraes determinou que o fim da proibição de visitas deveria ser comunicado à Secretaria de Segurança Pública do Distrito Federal e ao diretor do Núcleo de Custódia da Polícia Militar do DF, que supervisionam a prisão do ex-presidente.

Nessa segunda (12), Flávio comemorou a decisão do STF, após participar de uma missa na Catedral de Brasília em homenagem ao Dia de Nossa Senhora Aparecida.

"Fiquei muito feliz que, no dia de Nossa Senhora Aparecida, é o dia que eu estou novamente autorizado a visitar o meu pai, vítima de uma injustiça. Hoje é só pra agradecer a Deus, agradecer a todo mundo que tá orando que tá rezando pelo nosso Brasil", declarou Flávio.

"Estou ansioso, são mais de três meses sem poder vê-lo por uma decisão, obviamente, sem critério nenhum, nenhum amparo legal", completou o candidato do PL, criticando a restrição que havia sido imposta pelo ministro do STF.

articles.title: Nunes Marques reúne campanhas de Lula e Bolsonaro sobre 2º turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente do TSE convocou equipes dos presidenciáveis na disputa para discutir condutas nas eleições. Decisões de Nunes Marques têm sido alvo de críticas das duas campanhas.
articles.summary: Nunes Marques reúne campanhas de Lula e Bolsonaro para discutir condutas no segundo turno após críticas de ambos os candidatos à atuação do tribunal.
articles.body:
O presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral, ministro Kassio Nunes Marques, se reúne nesta terça-feira (13) com os coordenadores de campanha dos candidatos Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), que disputam o segundo turno das eleições para a Presidência.

A ideia do encontro é discutir as condutas no segundo turno. Nas últimas semanas, as campanhas dos presidenciáveis geraram uma disputa de liminares no TSE.

O episódio mais recente foi o impasse gerado pelo canal "Exército do Lula" no WhatsApp, que chegou a ser suspenso e, horas depois, restabelecido (relembre mais abaixo).

Neste caso, a palavra final será do plenário. Porém, tanto Lula quanto Bolsonaro reclamaram das decisões do TSE no caso.

Lula questionou a conduta do presidente da Corte Eleitoral nessa segunda (12) e disse que o TSE não pode ter "lado na política". Também afirmou que alguns ministros estão "extrapolando em algumas decisões contra a minha campanha. Isso é visível. Já foi denunciado".

A campanha de Flávio, por sua vez, divulgou uma nota em que afirma que o canal de WhatsApp ligado ao petista utiliza estratégias de apagamento sistemático de mensagens e uso de links para burlar o controle da Justiça Eleitoral e prometeu enviar um novo relatório de provas.

Ministro Kassio Nunes Marques — Foto: Luiz Roberto/TSE

Nessa segunda-feira (12), a equipe técnica do TSE afirmou, em análise produzida a pedido do presidente da Corte, Nunes Marques, que não encontrou as notícias falsas denunciadas pela campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro contra o senador no canal "Exército do Lula", criado para mobilizar eleitores do candidato à reeleição nas redes sociais.

"Não foram localizadas novas publicações que reproduzam os conteúdos examinados nos autos ressalvando o conteúdo de vídeos que, pela urgência, não foram transcritos", diz o relatório.

O documento foi produzido após um impasse envolvendo o canal na Corte Eleitoral. No domingo (11), Nunes Marques determinou a suspensão do canal, após um pedido da campanha de Flávio que alegou que o canal era usado para disseminar fake news contra o adversário de Lula nas urnas.

Horas depois, o corregedor-geral da Justiça Eleitoral, ministro Ricardo Villas Bôas Cueva, suspendeu a ordem do presidente da Corte, Nunes Marques, e reabilitou o funcionamento do canal de WhatsApp. A nova decisão é preliminar e deverá ser discutida pelo plenário do TSE.

Ricardo Villas Bôas Cueva determinou a suspensão da decisão porque o caso estava sob relatoria dele. O corregedor, no entanto, proibiu a divulgação de conteúdos falsos que já tenham sido analisados pelo tribunal. Em caso de descumprimento, o canal poderá ser suspenso novamente.

Ele também determinou que o caso seja discutido em plenário, antes de uma determinação definitiva sobre o canal.

articles.title: Caso Master: Fachin recebe relatórios da PF sobre ministros do STF | G1
articles.standfirst: Alas de Moraes e Mendonça defendem que presidente do Supremo envie elementos de todos citados para avaliação da PGR, numa tentativa de arrefecer embates.
articles.summary: No Caso Master, Fachin recebe relatórios da PF que citam ministros do STF, enquanto alas da Corte sugerem envio dos dados à PGR para reduzir tensões.
articles.body:
O presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), Edson Fachin, se reúne com o diretor-geral da Polícia Federal (PF), Andrei Rodrigues, nesta terça-feira (13) para discutir menções a integrantes da Corte no caso Master.

O material foi requisitado por Fachin ao diretor-geral da PF, Andrei Rodrigues, ao confirmar uma reunião, que foi pedida pelo delegado. Em um ofício, Fachin afirmou que nenhum fato nem ninguém deve ficar fora da apuração.

Dos 10 ministros do Supremo, há citações, em graus diferentes, de pelo menos seis ministros ou parentes — além de referências a ministros do Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ) e do Tribunal Superior do Trabalho (TST).

Ministro Edson Fachin do STF — Foto: Rosinei Coutinho/STF

A movimentação da PF tem potencial para aprofundar a crise instalada no Supremo desde setembro, pressionando Fachin a adotar providências em relação aos colegas.

Até agora, o foco estava nos ministros Alexandre de Moraes e André Mendonça, que diante das costuras internas expuseram publicamente a divisão da Corte.

A PF avalia que o encontro pode resolver eventuais divergências provocadas pelo caso Master com o Supremo e pavimentar a retomada das investigações. Nas últimas semanas, a PF trabalhou na individualização das citações.

A ala do ministro Alexandre de Moraes defende que não haja avanços antes do fim das eleições. A avaliação desses ministros é que, com um cenário mais completo sobre o que de fato a PF entende ter reunido contra cada integrante da Corte, cabe ao Presidente do Supremo dar o mesmo tratamento a todos os citados.

Nos bastidores, aliados de Moraes e do ministro André Mendonça afirmam reservadamente que o melhor caminho seria a Presidência enviar os elementos reunidos pela Polícia Federal para análise da Procuradoria-Geral da República, sem vincular a medida ao procurador-geral, Paulo Gonet, que também foi citado no caso e teve uma apuração rejeitada pelo Conselho Superior do Ministério Público.

O encaminhamento dos casos para a PGR, além de dar respaldo ao Supremo para decidir diante de uma análise técnica, ainda daria tempo para novas investidas para uma composição interna — apontada ainda como de difícil solução.

Ministros, no entanto, apontam que houve uma certa melhora no clima entre as duas alas após o primeiro turno, mas que Mendonça e Moraes ainda estão sem se falar, assim como Gilmar Mendes e Nunes Marques.

As ligações de ministros do STF com o caso Master começaram em abril de 2025, quando a colunista Malu Gaspar, do jornal "O Globo", revelou a contratação do escritório da mulher do ministro Alexandre de Moraes pelo Banco Master para representação em algumas ações.

Em dezembro, foi publicado que o contrato era de cerca de R$ 130 milhões e, neste ano, a PF apontou que o ministro foi interlocutor ao menos de 52 mensagens de Vorcaro, inclusive no dia em que foi preso.

Depois, surgiram negócios que envolviam o ministro Dias Tóffoli com fundos do Banco Master na sociedade de um resort da família do ministro no Paraná, o que levou o ministro a deixar a relatoria do caso Master e a se declarar suspeito para analisar questões da investigação na Segunda Turma do Supremo.

No mês passado, surgiram mensagens que citavam envolvimento com Daniel Vorcaro, do ministro Nunes Marques, do filho dele, também envolvendo contratações, e do filho do ministro Luiz Fux, por susposto pedido de ajuda em um processo.

Em relação ao ministro André Mendonça, foi divulgada uma foto com advogado de Vorcaro, um encontro com o banqueiro e um pedido de investigação de uma possível relação entre o Banco Master e o Instituto Iter — ligado ao ministro. Também foi identificada a contratação de Chiquinho Feitosa, ex-cunhado do ministro Gilmar Mendes, por Vorcaro, além de uma reunião e tentativas de aproximação.

Todos os ministros e familiares negam irregularidades ou envolvimentos com Daniel Vorcaro.

articles.title: US military archbishop urges Catholic soldiers to refuse involvement in Army firing squad execution
articles.summary: Archbishop Timothy Broglio urged Catholic soldiers to refuse firing squad duty in the planned execution of Nidal Hasan, calling the livestream barbaric.
articles.body: Catholics serving in the Army should request to be excused from participating in the planned firing squad execution of a convicted Fort Hood mass shooter, which the Pentagon has proposed livestreaming, a prominent U.S. archbishop who oversees Catholic pastoral services for the military said on Monday. Archbishop Timothy Broglio raised several objections to the Pentagon's unprecedented plan to broadcast the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base. Hasan, now 56, uses a wheelchair after being shot by responding officers during the attack. Hasan is set to be executed at Fort Hood on Dec. 3, at 1 p.m. CST, according to the U.S. Army, which would make him the first person to be executed by firing squad by the U.S. military since 1945. It would also mark the first U.S. military execution by any method since 1961. Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth said he wanted soldiers to execute Hasan at the time, day of the week and location of the shooting and has argued that making the execution public would help serve as a deterrent. Broglio recalled presiding over the funeral of one of Hasan's victims, Michael Grant Cahill, the only civilian killed in that attack, and expressed sorrow over the deadly shooting. But the archbishop questioned whether the U.S. government wanted to "imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries." POPE LEO DENOUNCES DEATH PENALTY AS 'INADMISSIBLE' AHEAD OF PENTAGON'S PLANNED LIVESTREAMED EXECUTION Hasan's crime "was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?" Broglio asked in a statement. "I oblige any Catholics assigned to the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church," he continued. Army regulations permit soldiers to seek religious exemptions or accommodations. It is unclear how the military intends to select members for the firing squad. "The U.S. military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world," Broglio said. "Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheelchair to the whole world?" A U.S. government execution has never been broadcast to the public, making it an unprecedented plan that has drawn backlash from political and religious leaders. Broglio joins other Catholic leaders in criticizing the Pentagon's plans to livestream the execution. The head of the U.S. bishops conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley, expressed "shock" and "great sorrow" about the public execution plan and urged the U.S. to reconsider. "In no way can Hasan’s actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he said in a statement on Friday. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people." Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, called the proposed broadcast "truly incomprehensible" and warned that it was "unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle." "The Church’s position is one of total opposition to the death penalty; it is incompatible with human dignity and serves as no deterrent," Parolin told reporters on Friday. According to the English translation published by Vatican News, Parolin said, "It is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this method in this day and age. I do not know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle. However guilty the person may be, there are other ways." Pope Leo XIV reiterated the Catholic Church's opposition to the death penalty as "inadmissible" in a social media post on Saturday marking World Day Against the Death Penalty. Citing Catholic doctrine revised under his predecessor, Pope Francis, Leo emphasized that the death penalty violates human dignity. "The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person. The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption," Leo, the first American pope, wrote on X without specifically mentioning the Pentagon's execution plan for Hasan. articles.title: LIZ PEEK: Two troubled Senate races could spoil Democrats' blue-wave fantasy
articles.summary: James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed face tightening senate races as past comments and shifting positions give Republican opponents new ammunition.
articles.body: The midterm elections are three weeks away. In some states, voting has already begun. Betting site Kalshi shows odds of 61% that Democrats will win control of the Senate. Recent developments in the Texas and Michigan races suggest keeping your money in your pocket. As voters find out more about front-runner Democrats James Talarico in Texas and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, the polls are tightening. They say intimacy breeds contempt; nowhere is this truer than in politics. KEN PAXTON CALLS OUT JAMES TALARICO'S 11-DAY ABSENCE AT TRUMP RALLY, PROMPTING RESPONSE FROM CAMPAIGN Talarico is the 2026 version of 2018 Senate wannabe Beto O’Rourke, who memorably live-streamed his teeth-cleaning as a campaign stunt, but ultimately lost to Republican Ted Cruz despite his laudable dental hygiene. Talarico, a photogenic 37-year-old state representative, recently vanished from public view for nearly two weeks, an extraordinary absence so close to Election Day. He says he had the flu; does he not know about Theraflu? Has he heard of Zoom? His disappearance gave rise to a whirlwind of apparently erroneous rumors. Because Talarico has voiced some wacky ideas in the past, like believing there are six genders or that God is non-binary — which he has been forced to walk back — some voters are primed to believe such rumors. 'FAKE' MODERATE TALARICO'S TEXAS SURGE TESTS PAXTON IN FIGHT TO HOLD CRUCIAL GOP SENATE SEAT Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, is an unpopular candidate and carries considerable baggage, but his well-funded campaign is running ads showing Talarico making incendiary comments like, "I always think of myself as a Christian who hates Christianity." Talarico has also been outed as having previously voted as a state representative against bans on biological men playing in women’s sports. Oops. Beto O’Rourke lost in part because he embraced aggressive gun control in a state where most people have a gun. In 2022, Talarico appeared with the Texas Humane Legislation Network, warning of the "existential" need to "reduce our meat consumption," in a state that prides itself on its cattle. Undoubtedly, Talarico’s progressive young base will not be deterred by his peculiar walk-about, but his lengthy absence from the campaign trail casts a cloud over his run. Some polls show him barely leading Ken Paxton; a recent UMass Lowell/YouGov poll shows the candidates tied, with 7% undecided. As Trump rallies to energize his still-faithful base, it’s hard to imagine Talarico pulling out the win. FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS Abdul El-Sayed, who calls himself a doctor, but is not legally authorized to practice medicine, has been changing positions as frequently as people change their underwear. One of the central planks in his platform has been his enthusiastic endorsement of Medicare for All. In a podcast from 2020, he says Medicare for All "does away with the private insurance market." Nowadays, his campaign website says: "Medicare for All does not have to ban additional private insurance through unions or employers, although Medicare for All should make those choices redundant and unnecessary." Moreover, during his primary race in January, El-Sayed explained, "If you like your insurance from your employer or from your union, that can still be there for you." That sounds a lot like President Obama telling gullible voters: "If you like your healthcare plan, you’ll be able to keep your healthcare plan, period." After millions of Americans saw their plans cancelled, Politifact dubbed that whopper the 2013 Lie of the Year. Why the reversal from El-Sayed on his signature issue? First, unions. Organized labor has done a bang-up job of demanding expensive healthcare benefits for workers — benefits that are undoubtedly more generous than any that would be provided by Uncle Sam. There are half a million union members in the Wolverine State; he needs their vote, ideals be damned. Second, those pesky taxes. El-Sayed has had to explain how he intends to pay for government-run healthcare. A writer at The Bridge, a nonpartisan news organization in Michigan, notes that "In 2020, the nonpartisan Urban Institute estimated that U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders’ version of Medicare for All would cost the federal government $34 trillion over a 10-year period." Experts say that money to fund such a program would rope in not just the wealthy, but middle-class families as well. In short, Medicare for All would mean higher taxes for all. El-Sayed has admitted as much in the past. El-Sayed positions himself as a healthcare expert, given his role in local county offices, but those stints were arguably brief and inconsequential. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Also troubling is El-Sayed’s association with anti-American Muslim organizations and personalities whom he has refused to denounce, like supporter Hasan Piker. On "Meet the Press" recently, El-Sayed claimed that neither he nor any family members have ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, a group deemed a terror outfit by the UAE, Saudi Arabia and by Egypt. But the candidate’s half-sister, an assistant professor at the University of Chicago, stated the opposite, claiming on social media years ago that her family "has long been" members of the Muslim Brotherhood and that some relatives had been "jailed" because of their association with the group. El-Sayed is also facing scrutiny for claiming dual citizenship with Egypt and the U.S. in the past, an assertion he now denies. El-Sayed told a Detroit GlobeMed conference in 2016, "I carry dual citizenship, and I grew up spending most of my summers in another country …" He made the same claim on his academic resume. Was he lying then, or is he lying now? Also, recently, asked during a debate whether El-Sayed considers Iran, the world’s biggest sponsor of terror, or Israel a bigger threat to the United States, the progressive anti-Israel candidate refused to answer. For many, his equivocation is disqualifying. articles.title: Media narrative predicting blue wave in key battleground state not meshing with local Republicans: 'Fired up'
articles.summary: Iowa Republicans in Scott County push back on "blue wave" predictions, citing voter optimism and concerns about Democratic spending ahead of midterms.
articles.body: DAVENPORT, Iowa — As Iowa emerges as one of the most critical states in the midterm election in both House and Senate races, Fox News Digital spoke with local Republican candidates about what the media is getting right and wrong on the ground in the Hawkeye State. As local conservatives gathered at a Scott County Republican Party event near downtown Davenport in early October to watch the first gubernatorial debate, a month out from the consequential midterm election, Fox News Digital was there asking if the media narrative was accurate that Iowa was primed for a "blue wave" amid concerns about President Donald Trump’s economy, gas prices, and the war in Iran. Greg Guy, running as a Republican for treasurer in Scott County, acknowledged that Iowans are "concerned" about the price of gas, but believes they understand that the surge in cost is likely temporary after the war in Iran winds down. "Surprisingly not," Guy said when asked if he thinks a blue wave is imminent in Iowa based on the reactions he gets when he knocks on doors in the county telling voters about his campaign, which he says is focused on doing "what’s right" and "taking care" of the community. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT "My neighbor is one of the big people in charge of the canvassing for the Democrat Party. I don't see where they're excited to vote," Guy said. "I mean, if I talk to a hundred doors and 30 to 40% will open up, I might get one out of 40. That's a hater, and then I'll just tell them, hey, I know you're not going to vote for me, but when I'm treasurer, and you have a problem, you can still call me. They don't know what to do because they're wound up in the hate. But otherwise, I don't think there's a whole lot of belief that the Democrat Party can do anything to fix our economy." Davenport, a town of about 100,000 people in southeast Iowa along the banks of the Mississippi River, stands out as a Democratic-leaning urban pocket in an increasingly Republican Iowa. President Trump carried Scott County by roughly four points in 2024, 51% to 47%, but former Vice President Kamala Harris won Davenport’s congressional district precincts overall, reflecting the city’s more competitive and complex political profile. Trump won Iowa by about 13 points in 2024, and Republicans control the governor’s office and both chambers of the state legislature. But Scott County’s mix of urban Democrats, suburban swing voters and conservative rural communities makes it a key test of whether the GOP’s statewide strength can overcome Democratic resilience in eastern Iowa. One of the critical questions is whether conservative Iowans are frustrated enough with Republicans to vote Democrats back into power. "No, not at all," Cynthia Mensendick, a registered nurse running for election to the Iowa State Senate to represent District 49, said when asked if voters think handing Democrats control of Congress is the "right answer." "The concern is that there will be a Democrat governor because if you look at any state where a Democrat takes over, they immediately increase spending," Mensendick said, adding, "I’m not seeing that," when asked if a "blue wave" was set to occur in Iowa this November. Mensendick, who is running a campaign focused on healthcare and the high cancer rate in Iowa, says one of the top concerns with Republican voters is Iowa turning into Illinois if Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand is elected. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: THE BIGGEST SURPRISES COME AFTER OCTOBER Republicans are facing an uphill battle in Iowa, where polling shows Democrats have gained momentum in the gubernatorial, Senate and congressional races. Additionally, Republicans are going up against historical headwinds as the party in power heading into the midterms. However, Iowa has shifted more red in recent years, and the Republicans in the room in Scott County remained optimistic. Dillon Fillion, the youngest candidate in Scott County history at 22 years old, told Fox News Digital that Republicans in Iowa and nationwide have a choice between two very different parties at the end of the day. "I think people have got to weigh the options here, they either have an option of voting for socialist candidates like Abdul El-Sayed, who is a pronounced communist and supports all the things that Lenin supports, which led the Soviet Union into the downfall that it went to, or they have the support of supporting Republicans who were actually serious about cutting their taxes, which cut their taxes in 2025 with the One Big Beautiful Bill," Fillion, running for the Iowa House of Representatives in District 81, said. "And Democrats will continue to lie about that, but again, the Democrats also voted to raise their taxes 60% in 2025, voting against the Big Beautiful Bill." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Kurt Whalen isn’t running for office, but rather serves as the Scott County Iowa GOP Vice Chair, and he told Fox News Digital that while there are many frustrations with the state of affairs from Republicans in the state, he doesn’t think GOP voters will sit on the sidelines with so much at stake. "I think people are still fired up for the Republican cause. I mean, we are a big tent party. There's people that absolutely love Trump, there’s people that don’t care for him. But the reality is, Trump's been an overwhelming force for good in our country," Whalen said. "So, we can haggle about specifics, but I really think the Republican Party will ultimately come home and certainly support the president, and I would certainly encourage them to do that because what other choice do we have? I mean, the other choice is straight up, communist, Marxist, DSA, mask mandates. The Democratic Party in general, if you look at it historically, it has always been for big government against the little guy."

articles.title: GOP senator said gas prices would decide the midterms. Now they’re threatening his reelection
articles.summary: Kansas Republican Sen. Roger Marshall boldly declared in July that “the midterms will be decided by the price of gasoline in October.”
articles.body:
Republican Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas boldly declared in July that "the midterms will be decided by the price of gasoline in October."

That prediction now looks strikingly prescient — though not in the way Marshall may have hoped: October has arrived with gasoline prices sharply higher, and Republican candidates across the country facing surprisingly competitive races.

Since the war in Iran began in late February, the average price of gasoline in the US has risen by about 46%, driven largely by disruptions to global oil markets caused by the war that many Republicans, Marshall included, have consistently defended.

In Kansas, the change is even more stark, with gas and diesel prices up more than 57% and 77%, according to AAA data.

As Republicans have started to adjust their messaging around the war, millions of dollars in political spending are also being redirected in a sign that the GOP is attempting to shore up its defense in reliably Republican states.

Marshall is the top beneficiary of that shift, as Republican super PACs pour millions of dollars into Kansas. Much of that money had been intended for North Carolina, where GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley has long been trailing in polls.

Senate Leadership Fund, one of the main Republican groups supporting Senate candidates, has booked nearly $10 million worth of ads in Kansas, according to AdImpact.

That last-minute investment underscores how Marshall's unequivocal support for the war — including his insistence that its economic costs were worth bearing — has become a real liability in a state that hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.

Marshall finds himself in an unexpectedly close contest with Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton, a pastor and founder of the nation's largest Methodist congregation.

In comments from the last several months reviewed by CNN's KFile, Marshall consistently argued that the war was worth the economic toll. He said Americans would have to "make some sacrifices" and that national security was "even more important than your pocketbook," later adding that keeping Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon was "worth the price."

Marshall himself has repeatedly acknowledged gas prices as an electoral liability, calling them "absolutely the barometer for this election" in June .

Gasoline prices in Kansas are still lower than the national average, but they have risen faster overall since the war began, eroding some of the state's advantage of having cheaper fuel. Today, Kansas gasoline averages about $4.01 a gallon and diesel about $6.01, according to AAA Fuel Prices. Gas is up from roughly $2.55 a gallon in the state from just before the war began, amounting to increases of about 57.5% for regular gasoline and about 77.6% for diesel.

Rising diesel prices are particularly consequential for Kansas farmers, who rely on that fuel to operate tractors and trucks during the fall harvest and winter wheat planting season. The increased costs come as farmers are already grappling with higher fertilizer expenses and tight operating margins.

While some Republicans in tough Senate races have backed away from support for the war, Marshall's support remains steadfast.

The Marshall campaign did not reply to CNN's request for comment.

When asked about rising gas prices in an interview with CNN's Kaitlan Collins in March shortly after the war with Iran began, Marshall answered that "Freedom is not free. Americans are going to have to make some sacrifices."

"We're the largest producer of oil in the world, that we are the second biggest exporter of oil in the world," Marshall said. "So, we're not going to be shut out economically from this … but this is one of the prices of war."

In an April interview with Newsmax , Marshall was asked about energy prices and how long America would be willing to pay high energy costs. Marshall compared it to sacrifices during World War II.

"We have to do it until we get the outcome that we want," he said. "I hope it's weeks and not months. But at the end of the day, Americans are gonna be safer."

"So, I'm sorry the gas prices are going up, but help is on his way," Marshall added. "And your national security, yes, is even more important than your pocketbook."

A day later, Marshall took that argument directly to farmers in his home state, acknowledging the strain of higher fuel and fertilizer costs while warning that the economic consequences could be far worse if Iran obtained a nuclear weapon and controlled the Strait of Hormuz.

"If this theocracy in Iran continues, and they develop a nuclear weapon and they control the strait, diesel fuel is going to go up to $15 a gallon and your fertilizers go up another 50% as well," Marshall said on RFD-TV , a channel dedicated to rural issues. "We hope this is short term. I appreciate the sacrifice the American farmer is making," he continued.

By late May, Marshall was still predicting that the economic fallout would be temporary. In an interview with Fox Business, he urged Americans "to stand behind the president, stand behind the commander in chief, stand behind our troops," adding, "I do think this war will be over sooner than later, and those gas prices will come back down."

"We cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon," he said.

The following month, Marshall pointed to the Trump administration's new memorandum of understanding with Iran as evidence that both the war and its economic consequences were easing.

"Americans are done with forever wars. Americans deserve affordable gas and groceries, and this agreement accomplishes just that," Marshall said in a June CNN interview, adding that gas prices were falling as the Strait of Hormuz reopened.

"I believe the benefits outweigh the risks," Marshall said on CNBC that same month.

The agreement quickly unraveled. By early July, negotiations had stalled, fighting had resumed and President Donald Trump declared the memorandum of understanding "over."

In July, Marshall was openly acknowledging the political stakes of high fuel prices.

On a local radio station, he said "the midterms will be decided by the price of gasoline in October," before arguing for swifter action: "So, I think if we're going to do something, we got to rip the Band-Aid off and just go in there."

And in August, Marshall told that same local radio station , "We want [the war] to be done tomorrow, but on the other hand, we can't allow Iran to have nukes. So this may be the price."

Last week, the Cook Political Report shifted the Kansas Senate race from "Lean Republican" to "Toss Up."

And while Marshall spent much of the spring predicting the war's economic consequences would be temporary, gasoline prices remain elevated just weeks before Election Day.

It leaves Marshall confronting the very political test he predicted in July, when he said that the midterms would be decided by the price of gasoline in October.

articles.title: Booker ‘wowed’ by GOP challenger’s blunt message to Trump
articles.summary: Justin Murphy told Trump to "finish it" on Iran, drawing applause and a stunned reaction from Cory Booker during their New Jersey Senate debate.
articles.body: Sen. Cory Booker’s Republican Senate challenger had a blunt message for President Donald Trump about the war in Iran during the pair’s recent debate: "Finish it." The advice drew applause during Thursday's forum — and a "Wow" from Booker, who then blasted former Tabernacle Deputy Mayor Justin Murphy's remarks as the kind of "Yahoo" foreign policy that has dragged the United States into costly wars in the Middle East. New Jersey is a blue state that has trended redder in recent years, with President Donald Trump flipping key areas in 2024. However, 1972 was the last time a Republican won a U.S. Senate election in the state, when Sen. Clifford Case was re-elected. Sens. Nick Brady in 1982 and Jeff Chiesa in 2013 later served brief, appointed terms. Murphy, an attorney from the Pine Barrens, earned loud applause for his response to a question about Iran when asked what he would tell Trump if the president called him for advice on the conflict. "Finish that war in a positive manner," Murphy replied firmly. "We can't wait halfway through and decide we don't want to do this anymore. The Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is a radical terrorist organization that has deprived the Iranian people, the Persian people, of their history and of a decent life." ‘FINISH THE DAMN JOB’: HAGERTY TELLS 'RUTHLESS PODCAST' THAT TRUMP WILL COMPLETE IRAN MISSION The exchange highlighted the candidates' opposing approaches to the conflict, with Murphy defending Trump's military campaign and Booker warning against another prolonged American war in the Middle East. As Murphy continued, the broadcast's split-screen showed Booker briefly looking down and shaking his head before pursing his lips for the rest of Murphy’s response and raising his eyebrows at one point. LAWMAKER’S STUNNED FACE AND OTHER VIRAL MOMENTS CAP ROUGH WEEK FOR POLITICAL CLASS "Four decades is enough. The Iranian people have suffered enough," Murphy began to conclude. "And I would say, ‘Mr. President, put your cowboy hat on and get out there and kick some a--, and get this done and done right’," Murphy said. "Wow," Booker mouthed as moderator David Wildstein gestured toward the Democrat and said it appeared he wanted to respond. BOOKER SLAMS TRUMP’S IRAN DEAL AS AN 'ABJECT SURRENDER,' LABELS HIM THE 'BIGGEST LOSER' WITH 'EGG ON HIS FACE' "Honestly," Booker began. "This is the kind of ‘Yahoo’ foreign policy that has mired us in Middle East war after Middle East war — with false bravado leaders saying we're just going to go in there and kick ass. Well, you know what that's done to the treasury of our country?" Booker replied. When asked the same question as Murphy, Booker joked that Wildstein was asking him about "a guy calling me for advice who has literally said ‘I know more than my generals’." But the former Newark mayor entertained the hypothetical, saying he and the rest of New Jersey have known Trump for years because he "bankrupted our casinos" — referring to the president’s former Atlantic City casino businesses. He accused Trump of frequently ignoring advice, claiming advisers had to "jangle keys" to keep him on topic during a meeting about the trans-Hudson rail tunnel project spearheaded by Booker and Sen. Charles Schumer, D-N.Y. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Murphy also received attention for his comments during the debate on illegal immigration. He recounted leaving a campaign event in Washington, N.J., and looking across at a home where a child was allegedly abducted and raped by Guatemalan illegal immigrant Lester Noe Perez-Amador — whom the Biden administration previously released after a Texas county notified ICE that it had taken him into custody, according to WRNJ. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Besides putting a Republican running for a long-held blue seat on the social media radar, the exchange over Iran underscored sharp divisions across party lines and within the Republican Party over Trump’s military campaign and how it should end.

articles.title: Hinson, Turek set to clash in second Iowa Senate debate
articles.summary: Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek (D) and Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) are set to clash in their second debate on Tuesday as they fight to succeed retiring Sen. Joni Ernest (R-Iowa). The debate will offer the candidates a chance to reiterate their stances on the Iran war and fuel prices, which proved to be a…
articles.body:
Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek (D) and Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) are set to clash in their second debate on Tuesday as they fight to succeed retiring Sen. Joni Ernest (R-Iowa).

The debate will offer the candidates a chance to reiterate their stances on the Iran war and fuel prices, which proved to be a focal point of their first debate last week.

WHO 13, a Des Moines news station owned by The Hill’s parent company, Nexstar Media, will host the debate. Moderated by WHO 13’s Amanda Krenz and KCAU’s Tim Seaman, it will focus on topics important to Iowa voters, according to Nexstar , such as immigration, education, health, agriculture and technology.

During the first debate , the pair notably highlighted their bipartisan records and times they broke from their respective parties — particularly Turek’s vote to criminalize some immigration violations and Hinson’s work with former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.).

A new survey from Emerson College Polling and The Hill released late last week had Hinson leading Turek and Libertarian candidate Thomas Laehn. Hinson notched 47 percent support, while Turek received 45 percent. Her lead is within the survey’s margin of error. Laehn received 2 percent support, and 7 percent of voters were undecided.

Laehn will not be participating, as he failed to meet Nexstar’s qualifying requirements.

Turek has garnered support from establishment Democrats, including former President Obama. In a video from the Turek campaign released in July, he battled the former president in a game of “IOWA” — a spin on the basketball game “HORSE.”

He has rejected support from former Vice President Harris, as with many red state Democrats, and has put focus on rising prices amid the ongoing war in Iran.

“We’re looking at diesel prices being at an all-time high as our farmers are going into harvesting time and leading to a furthering increase of input costs, like fertilizer,” Turek said during the first debate, adding Iowa farmers are telling him it affects their bottom lines.

Hinson has had to balance her links to President Trump amid his historically low approval ratings.

She called for the war in Iran to end, saying in the first debate that she wanted a quick end to prevent the further loss of American troops.

“I don’t want this to be a forever war, so I want to make sure we do everything we can,” Hinson said. “I trust in our U.S. military, the greatest fighting force in the world, to bring this to a close as quickly as possible, because I know people are getting squeezed.”

Decision Desk HQ , a partner of The Hill, stated on Monday that Hinson is “narrowly favored” over Turek. The Cook Political Report , a nonpartisan election handicapper, rates the race as a “toss-up.”

articles.title: MAGA’s theory of the electorate on the line in Ohio
articles.summary: Vice President Vance went back to his native Ohio last week to hold a rally and cast his early ballot in what have been — at least to many in the national political press — surprisingly difficult Senate and gubernatorial races for his party. They shouldn’t be so surprised. The big-ticket item is the Senate…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance went back to his native Ohio last week to hold a rally and cast his early ballot in what have been — at least to many in the national political press — surprisingly difficult Senate and gubernatorial races for his party.

The big-ticket item is the Senate seat Vance gave up to become President Trump’s number two.

Republican Jon Husted, then serving as Ohio’s lieutenant governor, was appointed to the seat last year. Husted was a sturdy choice: a political workhorse who had served as the Speaker of the Ohio House and won statewide elections in 2010 and 2014 as secretary of state before running for governor in 2018. He lost the primary but joined the ticket of the winner, Mike DeWine, for two very successful outings as his running mate.

Husted is in many ways the opposite of the man he replaced in the Senate. Husted is seen in both Columbus and Washington as a party loyalist, a dogged campaigner, a political professional and something of a dealmaker. He’s sort of the archetypal Ohio Republican, with a team peppered with John Boehner alums to prove it. If this were a good year to be a generic Republican in Ohio, Husted would be the man for the job.

But it isn’t a good year to be a Republican in Ohio — or pretty much any place that President Trump won by less than 15 points in 2024. That was the year that Husted’s Democratic challenger, Sherrod Brown, lost the Buckeye State’s other Senate seat to Republican Bernie Moreno, who, like Vance, ran as a mega-MAGA outsider and then rode Trump’s coattails to beat Brown by a little less than 4 points.

Brown, who has long emphasized his shirt-sleeved, everyman persona, is actually a lot like a Democratic version of Husted: lengthy statehouse tenure, two terms as Ohio secretary of state and lots of party dues paying. And in the Clinton and Obama eras when times were better for Ohio Democrats, Brown was ideally situated to become what seemed to be a permanent incumbent. His first three Senate runs — 2006, 2012 and 2018 — were all good years for Ohio Democrats. But in 2024, when Trump won Ohio by the widest margin of any presidential candidate since Ronald Reagan, Brown couldn’t hold on.

Like this year, we didn’t get much high-quality polling out of Ohio in 2024. But the surveys we did see showed Brown starting with a lead that faded in the fall. He was up 4 points at the end of September , tied in October and, finally, falling behind in the days just before the election . Brown still outperformed then-Vice President Kamala Harris, the Democratic presidential nominee, but only by a measly 3 points.

The Republicans’ theory of Ohio politics is that the 2024 election and, even more so, the 2022 midterm in which Vance won the seat Husted is now trying to defend, prove that Ohio is no longer a red-tinted swing state but rather a bright red one. In 2022, Vance was a controversial, polarizing figure who had never held elective office and still managed to beat longtime Democratic congressman Tim Ryan by 6 points.

The Democratic theory is that Ohio remains very politically elastic and that the large number of white, working-class voters in the state have been in a marriage of convenience with the Republican Party. Democratic strategists believe that with lots of older voters, a large number of Roman Catholic voters in the north and a big swath of Appalachia in the south, Ohio has been voting its values more than its pocketbook. (It’s not by accident that Husted’s campaign and its allies have focused so much on transgender issues .)

Democrats like Brown hold that the reason candidates like Trump and Vance have succeeded in Ohio is that they fuse economic and cultural populism in a way that progressive Democrats haven’t been able to match. The incumbent Republican Brown beat to get into the Senate in 2006, DeWine, is of the old down-the-line conservative model. DeWine, now the term-limited governor, has been a stellar vote-getter for state office, running 10 points ahead of Vance in 2022. DeWine’s success pokes holes in both the MAGA and Democratic views, but there’s certainly something to the idea of Ohio as a state that wants to be Democratic at work and Republican at home.

Under that view, Brown is ideally situated for a comeback this year since the overwhelming focus of voters in 2026 is economic, just like 20 years ago when he unseated DeWine amid a period of high energy prices and an unpopular Middle Eastern war.

And unlike in his 2024 loss, this time it’s been Brown who has been gaining ground. Picking from the sadly sparse selection of high-quality polls, we can see Brown trailing this summer before moving into the lead. Since June, no legitimate poll has shown Husted leading. And two recent high-quality surveys have put Brown at 49 percent of the vote, suggesting that there isn’t some trove of undecided voters that is going to sweep in and propel Husted to a big win.

That’s not to say that this is a done deal. Hardly. We don’t have enough good polls to do a useful average for this race, but Husted will almost certainly outperform his recent polls. The floor for a statewide Republican in Ohio these days seems to be something like 47 percent of the vote, which is certainly close enough to be well positioned for any late-cycle momentum shifts.

Of course, Vance isn’t the only one casting an early ballot. Ohio has set new records for preelection voting in both of its past two midterms. It was about 35 percent of the vote in 2022, and while most early voters are long-determined in their preferences, the late deciders are rapidly entering the chat.

The premise of Ohio as the Vance-ian heartland of the new working-class Republican Party is on the line, so MAGA had better hurry.

articles.title: 46 percent believe midterm vote will be counted accurately: NewsNation-DDHQ poll
articles.summary: A new poll released on Tuesday found that 46 percent of likely voters believe all the votes in the midterms will be counted accurately, underscoring how voter faith in elections has taken a hit. An exclusive NewsNation/Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) poll, conducted by AI research platform TrueDot.ai, found 27 percent of respondents said they were…
articles.body:
A new poll released on Tuesday found that 46 percent of likely voters believe all the votes in the midterms will be counted accurately, underscoring how voter faith in elections has taken a hit.

An exclusive NewsNation/Decision Desk HQ ( DDHQ ) poll, conducted by AI research platform TrueDot.ai, found 27 percent of respondents said they were only concerned about correctly counting mail-in ballots, while 14 percent said they believed Republicans would change the vote count. Another 13 percent said they believed Democrats would change the vote count.

Respondents were then asked if the issue of whether or not they believed all the votes would be counted accurately impacted their likelihood to vote. Forty-six percent left the question blank, though 29 percent said it had no impact, and 22 percent said it did and that they needed to vote to overwhelm the fraud.

Roughly 3 percent of respondents said that concern demoralized them and made them less likely to cast a ballot.

“Republicans have shown in recent years more doubt about election results, and obviously a lot of this has to do with the 2020 election and President Trump’s rhetoric surrounding it,” DDHQ chief elections analyst Geoffrey Skelley said.

Given that Trump is back in office, some Democrats are not necessarily inclined “to trust that results will be counted fairly as well,” he added.

The NewsNation/DDHQ poll was conducted by TrueDot.ai from Oct. 5 to 9 with 974 likely 2026 national voters. The margin of error for the full survey is 3.2 percentage points.

The full results of the poll will be discussed on “Decision Desk 2026 Have Your Say: A NewsNation Town Hall” hosted by Chris Cuomo on Tuesday night on NewsNation.

Former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel, broadcaster and commentator Stephen A. Smith and former Trump strategist Steve Bannon will discuss what they see in the numbers during the town hall.

articles.title: Democrats hold 7-point lead on generic congressional ballot: NewsNation-DDHQ poll
articles.summary: Democrats are leading Republicans on the generic congressional ballot by 7 points, according to a new poll — underscoring the Democrat-friendly environment three weeks out from Election Day. An exclusive NewsNation/Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) poll, conducted by AI research platform TrueDot.ai and released on Tuesday, showed Democrats leading Republicans with 49 percent support to the…
articles.body:
Democrats are leading Republicans on the generic congressional ballot by 7 points, according to a new poll — underscoring the Democrat-friendly environment three weeks out from Election Day.

An exclusive NewsNation/Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) poll, conducted by AI research platform TrueDot.ai and released on Tuesday, showed Democrats leading Republicans with 49 percent support to the GOP’s 42 percent on the generic congressional ballot, with a separate 8 percent of survey respondents undecided. NewsNation is owned by Nexstar, which also owns The Hill.

When respondents were asked which party has done more to earn their vote, regardless of whom they’re voting for, 46 percent said the Democratic Party while 40 percent said the GOP. Close to 7 percent said independents while 8 percent said none of the above.

The full results of the poll will be discussed on “Decision Desk 2026 Have Your Say: A NewsNation Town Hall” hosted by Chris Cuomo on Tuesday night on NewsNation.

Former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel, broadcaster and commentator Stephen A. Smith and former Trump strategist Steve Bannon will discuss what they see in the numbers during the town hall.

Recent polling has shown Democrats holding a steady and significant edge on the congressional ballot, with forecasters and analysts expecting the party to take back the House in November.

Decision Desk HQ forecasts that Democrats have a 76 percent probability of winning back the House while Republicans have a 24 percent probability of holding the lower chamber.

“The big question is if the lead grows more,” said Geoffrey Skelley, chief elections analyst at DDHQ.

“You’re basically out of time for much to change,” he added. “At this point, it is probably more just about engaging the voters in your party as best you can, and making some final cases to voters who might normally or might have in the past voted for your party, if you’re Republicans in particular, and then trying to make the case for why they should show up again.”

The NewsNation/DDHQ poll found President Trump with a 38 percent favorability rating, compared with a 60 percent unfavorable rating. Inflation (28 percent), jobs and the economy (20 percent) and immigration and the border (12 percent) ranked among what voters said are the most urgent issues facing the U.S.

Skelley said he was “very skeptical” that Trump’s recent deal with Russia to add 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and global marketplace would move voters before November. The deal has also caused some bipartisan backlash.

“Americans don’t … necessarily have a very popular opinion of Russia, and so some may look askance at this move as well,” he added.

Observers say Democrats’ chances of taking back the Senate, where they need to flip four seats, is a toss-up as they contend with Republican-friendly states such as Ohio, Alaska, Iowa and Texas. Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 56 percent chance of flipping the Senate and Republicans a 44 percent chance.

The NewsNation/DDHQ poll was conducted by TrueDot.ai between Oct. 5 and Oct. 9 with 974 likely 2026 national voters. The margin of error for the full survey is 3.2 percentage points.

articles.title: Candidates campaign for House seats in districts where they don’t live
articles.summary: A handful of congressional candidates are seeking office in districts where they do not live, putting their local ties in focus as the midterm election season heats up. In Arizona, Democrat Amish Shah and Republican Jay Feely are vying to represent the state’s 1st Congressional District despite both of them living outside its boundaries. A…
articles.body:
A handful of congressional candidates are seeking office in districts where they do not live, putting their local ties in focus as the midterm election season heats up.

In Arizona, Democrat Amish Shah and Republican Jay Feely are vying to represent the state’s 1st Congressional District despite both of them living outside its boundaries.

A similar dynamic is unfolding in New York, where Republican Rep. Nick LaLota and Democratic challenger Chris Gallant are competing in the 1st District. LaLota lives in Amityville, in the neighboring 2nd District, while Gallant resides in Amity Harbor.

These races, among others, underscore the distinction between the constitutional requirements for serving in Congress and voters’ expectations that their representatives have local ties. The Constitution requires House members to be inhabitants of the states they represent but does not require them to live within their congressional districts.

Antjuan Seawright, a Democratic strategist, however, told The Hill that it makes it hard for candidates living outside the districts they are campaigning in to get to know the “community and the people.”

“And so it puts both parties at a disadvantage,” Seawright said.

Some candidates have pledged to move into their districts if elected, while others have found themselves outside district lines because of redistricting.

In Virginia, for example, Democrat Elaine Luria is running for the 2nd Congressional District, which she represented in the House for two terms beginning in 2019. Luria lost to GOP Rep. Jen Kiggans in the 2022 midterms and is now fighting to win the seat back.

Virginia’s legislature — then led by Republicans — redistricted House lines in 2021, which Luria blames in part for her defeat.

“In 2020, when Elaine became the first Democrat in decades to win VA-02 two times in a row she scared Virginia Republicans so badly that they had to gerrymander her out of the district,” Zach Emanuel, a spokesperson for Luria’s campaign, said in a statement.

Luria is now running for the seat outside the district, given the redrawn lines. Independent candidate J. Matt Baker is also running for the seat while living outside the district.

Baker wrote on his website that his neighborhood was moved to Virginia’s 3rd District after the district boundaries were redrawn.

“I did not leave the district; the mapmakers simply shifted a line less than a mile to the east. My community and the people I identify with are unchanged. Fortunately, the law is clear, and I only need to be a resident of the state to run in the 2nd District. And there is nowhere else I would rather represent,” Baker wrote.

Redistricting isn’t an issue in Arizona or New York, where Democrats sought to redraw lines but had their map blocked in court.

Feely said in a statement that he and his wife are currently building a house in Arizona’s 1st District.

“Although 4 of 9 current Arizona congressional representatives don’t live in their district, we believe it’s important to be closer to those I hope to represent in Washington,” Feely said. “I’ve spent the last year on the campaign trail listening to voters from all corners of the district, and I’m running to address their concerns and deliver results in Congress.”

A source familiar with the matter said that Shah lives a mile outside the district and has represented portions of the district while serving in the Arizona state legislature.

The Hill had reached out to LaLota and Gallant’s campaigns for comment.

GOP analyst Rob Stutzman said a candidate’s address may matter less when a district and their surrounding area share the same broader community.

“For instance, if you’re in a massive suburban sprawl district in the Phoenix Metro, and you live outside that district, but you’re still essentially part of the same metro area, it may not be that distinguishing of a characteristic because it’s all one large type of community. We’ve seen this in California suburban districts,” Stutzman said.

The Republican analyst also said a candidate’s name recognition could help offset concerns about living outside a district, pointing to Feely’s status as a former professional football player.

“Someone like Feely, who’s maybe a bit of a celebrity candidate, right? You know, has some of that fame. Sometimes that overrides … and I don’t know exactly how that district is drawn, but … if it’s, you know, Mesa versus Chandler, you kind of don’t care as much because the guy’s from the area and he’s kind of got a bit of that fame aspect going for him,” Stutzman said.

Even so, candidates who live outside the districts they’re running to represent can also find themselves on the defensive, as opponents seize on their addresses to paint them as outsiders disconnected from local voters.

The Republican National Committee, for instance, put out a press release in August citing an article from the Washington Examiner that Luria bought a second home out of her district.

“Maybe Luria should ‘work out the logistics’ of actually living in the district she’s running to represent instead of lying to Virginians,” the committee wrote at the time.

articles.title: Why an El-Sayed win in Michigan is important for Ocasio-Cortez
articles.summary: As Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) considers whether she’ll run for president or seek a New York Senate seat, the outcome of Michigan’s Senate race pitting a progressive Democrat against a former GOP congressman could help shape her decision. Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed is battling former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) to succeed retiring Sen. Gary…
articles.body:
As Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) considers whether she’ll run for president or seek a New York Senate seat, the outcome of Michigan’s Senate race pitting a progressive Democrat against a former GOP congressman could help shape her decision.

Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed is battling former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.).

A win by El-Sayed would give progressives a tangible data point to bolster their argument that their brand of politics can win statewide — particularly in a critical battleground state like Michigan.

And the victory could be especially significant for Ocasio-Cortez, who is set to campaign with El-Sayed this week.

Ocasio-Cortez will join El-Sayed beginning Thursday on a two-day swing through Michigan where she will appear on his “It Shouldn’t Be This Hard” bus tour through the state’s Upper Peninsula. On Friday, she’ll appear in southeastern Michigan for campaign rallies at two colleges and a separate event with Latino voters.

A win by El-Sayed could strengthen the case for the congresswoman to launch a presidential bid in 2028 and build on that momentum, Democratic strategists say.

“The one race in 2026 that will impact what happens in 2028 is the Michigan Senate race,” said Democratic strategist Joel Payne. “That will set the tone for the 2028 primary field and will do a lot to prove theories from all sides of the Democratic coalition.”

While El-Sayed is not a democratic socialist, his campaign themes are very similar to Ocasio-Cortez’s on the economy and foreign policy — from supporting “Medicare for All” to harsh criticisms of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to calling for a change in the way the U.S. handles Israel.

If a candidate in Michigan can win statewide office on those issues, it bodes well for Ocasio-Cortez in a national race. And it would all suggest the wave of progressive politics that first elevated Ocasio-Cortez is growing stronger across the country.

Referring to Ocasio-Cortez specifically, one major Democratic donor put it this way: “I don’t see a world in which first [Democratic New York City Mayor] Zohran Mamdani wins, and then Abdul El-Sayed wins a year later, and she doesn’t take that as a cue for her own entree into the 2028 presidential primary.”

“It would be silly if all that happened and she looked the other way,” the donor said.

Ocasio-Cortez was candid about her decisionmaking process in an interview with The New York Times last month, telegraphing pretty clearly that she’s aware she may only have one go at a presidential run, nodding to the moment where progressives and democratic socialists have had some success in recent months.

“There’s an argument that some make that this is a very unique political window and, oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot,” the congresswoman told the Times.

But Ocasio-Cortez was even more direct about how she feels an El-Sayed win would translate to other races — including possibly her own.

Speaking at a fundraiser for El-Sayed in New York last week, according to audio obtained by ABC News, Ocasio-Cortez told attendees that a win by El-Sayed “would break open the entire political calculus in America — period.”

“Because if you can win, if Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere,” she said. “Anywhere.”

Recent polls show that Ocasio-Cortez is in the top five of potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders. She draws roughly 11 percent support in the RealClearPolling national average — coming in fourth place behind former Vice President Kamala Harris, California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

A July survey of likely Democratic voters in New Hampshire — which remains one of the early state primaries — shows her leading the field with 22 percent support.

Democratic strategist Jamal Simmons said it’s clear more progressive candidates are “having a moment” and Ocasio-Cortez could benefit from that support among the electorate.

But, Simmons said, “It’s unclear how much we overestimate the strength they’re having.”

“They’re winning but all Democrats are winning,” Simmons said. “Some of it is just anti-Trump fervor and in normal times it may not hold.”

Ocasio-Cortez, he said, is doing the “risk-reward analysis” of “go now or hold your fire,” and it’s unclear where she might end up.

“The probability for success in a Senate race is much greater” than a presidential race, he said. “But there’s a risk in waiting for it because she might not have another opportunity for a Senate seat for a while.”

Other Democrats say if El-Sayed wins Michigan, it may offer some clarity. But it doesn’t 100 percent answer the question of her being able to win in a somewhat blue but sometimes competitive presidential state, said Democratic strategist Eddie Vale.

“I think what she — and frankly everyone on the different sides of current ideological fights — are going to need to take the results of the midterms as providing important information, but not being decisive proof,” Vale said.

The donor, however, maintained that Ocasio-Cortez stands to benefit the most from an El-Sayed victory.

“If he wins, she comes out the clear winner,” the donor said. “And that will make it harder for her to say no.”
