articles.title: Trump picks fight with GOP senators over Russia diesel deal
articles.summary: President Trump is picking a fight with Senate Republicans right before the midterm elections with his surprise deal to allow Russia to export diesel to the United States. Four Republican senators — Sens. Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), John Curtis (Utah) and Thom Tillis (N.C.) — have already spoken out against the controversial deal…
articles.body:
President Trump is picking a fight with Senate Republicans right before the midterm elections with his surprise deal to allow Russia to export diesel to the United States.

Four Republican senators — Sens. Susan Collins (Maine), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), John Curtis (Utah) and Thom Tillis (N.C.) — have already spoken out against the controversial deal between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Many others are likely privately critical of the stunning move, which Trump executed without advanced warning or consultation with Republican senators.

“I think there are a lot more people that are privately critical of it. The question is whether they want to go public with it,” said Vin Weber, a GOP strategist and former member of the House Republican leadership.

The Senate just two months ago passed a tough Russia sanctions package, which Trump had delayed for months despite mounting pressure from fellow Republicans to embrace it.

“The bigger political risk for the president on this — if it’s a political risk — is there is a substantial base of support in his party for taking a very tough attitude on Russia which he does not seem to share,” said Weber.

As the days pass, more Republican senators are expected to condemn Trump’s deal with Russia, which will generate hundreds of millions of dollars for the Russian economy and could put it in a better position to continue the war against Ukraine. Under the deal, the U.S. would buy an estimated 2.5 million tons of fuel from Russia.

“The deep-seated support for Ukraine in this fight should not be underestimated [among] the Republicans or [among] America most broadly. Most Americans have spent their entire lives understanding that Russia is our rival at best and our flat-out enemy at worst,” Weber said. “They are deeply invested in supporting Ukraine emotionally and otherwise.”

Trump is facing pressure to do something about high fuel and diesel costs that have been driven up by the war in Iran.

One senior Senate Republican aide expressed hope that the deal could give crucial help to Republican candidates in the final sprint to Election Day.

“Trump realizes that diesel prices are very high, and I think he’s trying to do anything he can do get it down. He did a deal with the devil from the looks of it,” the source said.

Danielle Pletka, a distinguished senior fellow specializing in U.S. foreign and defense policy at the American Enterprise Institute, called the diesel deal “a lifeline for Putin” at a moment when the Russian offensive has stalled out in Ukraine.

But she suggested that Trump is “desperate” to bring down diesel prices as polls now show Democrats favored to win the House and possibly the Senate, too, in next month’s election.

“It’s just an act of desperation by a president who doesn’t see the optics,” she said, calling the lifting of sanctions “a lifeline for Putin at a moment he’s losing ground. Looks like a pact between two desperate men.”

Senators who voted for a tough new sanctions package against Russia aren’t happy about the prospect of the United States now buying hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel, particularly when they’d worked for months to stop China and India from buying Russian energy products.

Collins, who is in a tough reelection fight in a state Trump has lost in his three presidential runs, criticized the commander in chief for not adhering to the Russia sanctions legislation he signed into law last month.

“I oppose President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on the purchase of diesel from Russia. I was a cosponsor of the Russian sanctions law, which the President recently signed but is now not following,” Collins, who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, wrote on social media Sunday.

She joined three other Senate Republicans and three Democrats in a joint statement blasting Trump for flouting a 2022 statute banning Russian energy imports.

“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine. Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO allies,” Collins declared in a joint statement with fellow Republicans Murkowski, Tillis and Curtis, as well as Democratic Sens. Ron Wyden (Ore.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.) and Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.), who is also the ranking member on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

“President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law,” the senators declared, noting that the administration had failed to consult with Congress or offer an explanation to justify the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil as required by law.

Republicans acknowledge high diesel costs have become a major political headwind for GOP candidates in battleground races across the country.

Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) said Trump is wrestling with a tough issue.

“The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions. He’s balancing his effort to stop and end … Putin’s war in Ukraine and lowering prices for American families,” he said Sunday on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.”

Barrasso, one of Trump’s staunchest allies in the Senate, didn’t say whether he supported the deal with Putin and quickly pivoted to blaming Democrats for constraining domestic oil production.

He argued that the Russia sanctions bill that Congress passed earlier this year was intended to give Trump “flexibility and the firepower to use another tool against Vladimir Putin,” suggesting Congress gave the president full discretion over how to apply sanctions.

The senior Senate Republican aide noted that diesel prices have already fallen to $6.27 a gallon from the high of $6.53 a gallon in September.

“He’s just trying something to get the price down immediately as quick as he can. I’ve seen prices come down too at the pump,” the source said. “Whatever is happening, whether it’s something that Trump is doing or it’s happening naturally, it couldn’t come at a better time for him.

“If you look at all the battleground states, the price of diesel, the price of gas are going to be the two big drivers of how people in the middle are going to vote,” the aide added. “It will be huge for farmers around the country who are harvesting right now.”

But Alex Jacquez, senior vice president for policy, advocacy and research at the Washington-based economic policy think tank Groundwork Collaborative, said the price of diesel is likely to stay above $6 through Election Day.

Jacquez estimated the deal would generate approximately $400 million for the Russian economy.

“It’s certainly not insignificant,” he said, but added “it’s not going to be the make-or-break” development in Russia’s war effort, either.

The impact on the U.S. economy is also likely to be modest. Jacquez predicted a “minimal” impact on domestic diesel prices.

“While 300,000 metric tons — 2.2 billion barrels — sounds like it’s a lot of barrels, which is why Trump is announcing it as such, that’s like half a day of diesel demand in the United States,” he said.

Jacquez previously served as a special assistant to former President Biden for industrial policy and economy development at the National Economic Council.

articles.title: Trump's new press secretary faces first major test as White House briefing room enters new era
articles.summary: Katie Zacharia makes her White House press briefing room debut Tuesday, ending a weekslong stretch without a permanent press secretary at the podium.
articles.body: The White House is set to end a weekslong stretch without a permanent press secretary at the podium Tuesday when Katie Zacharia makes her briefing room debut, succeeding Karoline Leavitt after a shake-up in President Donald Trump's communications team. "I am pleased to announce that Katie Zacharia will be beginning her term as Press Secretary tomorrow, Columbus Day, and will be doing an introductory News Conference on Tuesday at 9:30 A.M. from the Press Briefing Room in the White House. Katie has been with me, in spirit, from the very beginning, and will do a fantastic job!" Trump said on Truth Social Sunday. Zacharia, an attorney and television commentator, served as senior communications adviser to Trump Media & Technology Group, which operates the president's social media platform, Truth Social. Her appointment follows Leavitt's departure from the White House in August. During his first administration, President Donald Trump had four White House press secretaries: Sean Spicer, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, Stephanie Grisham and Kayleigh McEnany. TRUMP NAMES LEAVITT SUCCESSOR AFTER WEEKS OF SPECULATION — AND SHE'S NO STRANGER TO MAGA Leavitt served as the first press secretary of Trump’s second administration for 19 months before leaving the role on Aug. 27. Zacharia previously served as deputy assistant secretary for public affairs and a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security. She appeared on "Fox & Friends Weekend" on Saturday in her new role, touting President Donald Trump's newly announced deal with Russia to supply more than 1.8 million tons of diesel fuel to U.S. and global markets in a bid to lower fuel and grocery costs. "President Trump has heard people have been frustrated with the gas prices. People are frustrated with the increasing grocery prices. And he is delivering what he always does, which are solutions," Zacharia said. KATIE ZACHARIA HITS GROUND RUNNING, PROMISES TRUMP DIESEL DEAL DELIVERS CHEAPER GAS FOR AMERICANS She celebrated the appointment in a post on X Friday, thanking Trump for what she called the "distinguished privilege" of serving as White House press secretary. "Serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime," Zacharia wrote. "President Trump has shown America that we can be great again, and he works to effectuate that greatness every single day. His confidence is a true privilege, and his leadership is a blessing to this country." "The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our Country and communicating to the American people the major wins that this Administration is making every single day," she wrote. "I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out," she added. She also acknowledged the expectations that come with succeeding Leavitt. KAROLINE LEAVITT JOINS FOX NEWS AS CONTRIBUTOR AFTER LEAVING WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY ROLE "Following the fabulous Karoline Leavitt is a high standard, and one worth meeting," Zacharia wrote. Since Leavitt's departure, the White House has held a limited number of press briefings and news conferences led by senior administration officials, including Vice President JD Vance and Attorney General Todd Blanche. The White House adopted a rotating lineup of top Trump administration officials to lead press briefings while Leavitt was on maternity leave over the summer. "Katie has been an effective champion of the MAGA movement and America First policies — and most importantly, clearly has [the] trust of President Trump," former Trump press secretary Sean Spicer told Fox News Digital on Friday. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Anyone who has not met her yet will quickly see that she is a genuinely kind person who will work well with the press corps, unlike the first press secretary who came across as an angry leprechaun at times," Spicer added, poking fun at himself.

articles.title: ‘Breaking Bad’ star RJ Mitte dies at 34, police say
articles.summary: “Breaking Bad” actor and advocate RJ Mitte is dead at the age of 34, the Brownsville Police Department confirmed Monday.
articles.body:
HARLINGEN, Texas ( KVEO ) — “Breaking Bad” actor and disability rights advocate RJ Mitte is dead at the age of 34, the Brownsville Police Department confirmed Monday.

The cause and manner of death remain under investigation, police say.

Mitte is known for his roles in various television shows including “Breaking Bad,” “The Oak Room,” “The Recall,” and “The Guardians of Justice.”

Mitte, who had cerebral palsy , is perhaps best remembered for his starring role as Walter White Jr. in “Breaking Bad.” Mitte starred alongside Bryan Cranston and Anna Gunn, who played his parents on the show.

Diagnosed at age 3, Mitte said in a 2014 interview that his disability and the surrounding struggles with physical therapy, family problems and exorbitant medical bills — all key subjects on the show – made him better at his job.

“You develop a different mentality, and you develop a different look at how the world sees you and how you see the world,” he continued at the time. “You’re able to use that. And I think it’s an asset instead of something that would hinder.”

“Breaking Bad” is widely considered to be one of the greatest shows of all time, according to viewers and experts .

As an advocate, he served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s. He was also president of his own Mitte Foundation supporting philanthropic and community initiatives around disabilities.

articles.title: US soldiers can't be protected from all bioweapons, Army admits amid troubling surge in threats
articles.summary: The U.S. Army's new biodefense plan integrates biological warfare scenarios into combat training as AI and biotechnology raise concerns about threats.
articles.body: The U.S. Army unveiled its plan to prepare soldiers to fight through biological attacks rather than assume every threat can be stopped. The newly signed plan bringing biological warfare scenarios into routine combat training as artificial intelligence (AI) and biotechnology raise new concerns about the weapons America's adversaries could develop in the near future. "Can we protect every soldier from every possible bio threat? Probably not," Dr. Alison Tamasi, a senior official at the Army's Nuclear and Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction Agency, told reporters on Monday. "We can't put them in a bubble," she added. The shift comes as U.S. officials continue to assess whether Moscow maintains an offensive biological weapons program after a mysterious death in Russia was linked to an anti-plague facility — reviving questions of biological safety and transparency. CHINESE AI MODEL INVESTIGATED AFTER RESEARCHER SAYS IT PROVIDED INSTRUCTIONS FOR BIOWEAPONS, ASSASSINATIONS Still, the Army hopes their implemented plan will help prepare the force to deploy and fight in biologically contested environments by 2035. Rather than treating outbreaks primarily as medical emergencies, the military wants commanders, intelligence officers and logistics personnel to prepare for biological threats while continuing to carry out their combat missions. EMERGING TECH HAS NEW ARMY LEADERS WARNING TROOPS CAN'T ‘AI’ THEIR WAY TO VICTORY ON THE BATTLEFIELD One of the biggest changes will be bringing biological incidents into major Army combat exercises, forcing commanders to respond to potential outbreaks while continuing their other missions. Rather than relying on specialized biological exercises, the Army wants troops across different military functions to confront biological threats as part of their regular training. Tamasi described one scenario involving a simulated norovirus outbreak at a military port. While medical personnel worked to contain the outbreak, logistics officers would have to determine how to keep critical supplies moving. The example illustrates a broader shift in the Army's approach: Biological threats are no longer being treated solely as medical problems but as potential disruptions to military operations that commanders must be prepared to manage. "We need to make sure that doctrine is aligned," Tamasi said, explaining that the Army is working to establish how biodefense readiness should be assessed across the force. The new plan, signed last week, puts into motion the Army's updated biodefense strategy released in September, which sets a goal of preparing soldiers to deploy and fight in biologically contested environments by 2035. The first two-year implementation cycle will focus on establishing policies, improving coordination across Army organizations and developing personnel with specialized biological expertise. More advanced technologies and acquisition efforts are expected in later phases. The effort comes amid growing concerns about the potential for artificial intelligence and biotechnology to accelerate the development of biological threats. PLAGUE MYSTERY REVIVES CONCERNS OVER NOT-TO-SECRET RUSSIAN BIOWEAPONS PROGRAM Tamasi described those advances as a dual-use challenge, with technologies that can accelerate medical discoveries also potentially enabling new biological threats to emerge more quickly. Russia remains a particular concern for U.S. national security officials. Washington has long assessed that Moscow maintains an offensive biological weapons program inherited from the Soviet Union, despite Russia's obligations under the Biological Weapons Convention. The United States renounced offensive biological weapons in 1969 and is also a party to the convention, which prohibits the development, production and stockpiling of biological weapons. US, WHO REQUEST DETAILS FROM RUSSIA AMID REPORTS OF SECOND PNEUMONIA CASE Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, died Oct. 2 after developing severe pneumonia. Russian media initially reported a possible pneumonic plague infection following a suspected laboratory accident, but Russian authorities denied that an accident occurred and said testing found no evidence of plague or other high-threat pathogens. The cause of her death remains undetermined. In an Oct. 10 update, the World Health Organization said it had found no evidence of ongoing transmission linked to the case, while noting that a confirmed diagnosis was still lacking. Asked how much Russia's biological weapons activities informed the Army's planning, Tamasi said the strategy was based on "intelligence writ large" rather than any single adversary. "It's not solely focused on a particular threat actor," she said. Asked what lessons the Army had drawn from Russia's biological weapons program, Tamasi said the strategy was designed to address biological threats regardless of their origin — whether accidental, deliberate or ultimately determined not to pose the threat initially feared. For Army commanders, she explained, the immediate priority is responding to a potential biological threat and maintaining operations, rather than determining its origin. Questions of attribution would involve the broader U.S. government. That approach also informs how the Army intends to detect emerging threats. Officials said the military is working to draw together information from environmental monitoring, medical facilities and intelligence reporting to identify potential biological incidents earlier. That could include wastewater surveillance similar to monitoring used during the COVID-19 pandemic, Tamasi said. The goal is to give commanders a more complete picture of potential biological threats so they can respond before disruptions spread. The COVID-19 pandemic also exposed the limitations of treating biological threats primarily as public health emergencies, according to Army officials, reinforcing the need for military leaders outside the medical field to incorporate those risks into operational planning. The strategy addresses misinformation as another operational challenge, particularly when troops and commanders must make decisions about vaccines, protective measures and communications during a biological incident. The Army has also begun rolling out biodefense seminars for senior leaders. Tamasi said one three-star board determined that senior Army leaders should receive at least an hour of instruction on biodefense and the "ground truth" surrounding biological threats. Ultimately, the Army hopes that preparing soldiers to continue their missions despite a biological attack could also discourage adversaries from using such weapons in the first place. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Tamasi said demonstrating that biological threats would not necessarily stop American forces from fighting could reduce the military advantage an adversary might hope to gain from deploying them.

articles.title: What I learned from interrogating Saddam Hussein
articles.summary: History can look very different depending on where you stand.
articles.body:
If someone had told me when I started working at CIA in February 1998 that one day I would be sitting in a darkened cell interrogating Saddam Hussein, I would have thought they were crazy.

Back then, Saddam was safely ensconced in power and, during the three years before the 9/11 terror attacks, it seemed to my CIA colleagues and me that it was only a matter of time before he got out from under the sanctions slapped on Iraq after the Gulf War and resumed a position of regional influence.

The terrorist attacks of September 11 in New York and Washington — and the Bush administration’s efforts to link Saddam to the attacks — showed CIA Iraq analysts that the U.S. and Iraq might be on a collision course that would culminate in war.

Interestingly, during my later conversations with Saddam, he told me that when he learned of the attacks, he had hoped that they would end the estrangement between the U.S. and Iraq. Surely, Saddam argued, Washington would see that his regime did not pose a threat to the U.S. — that we shared a common enemy in Sunni extremism. He could not have been more wrong.

Recently, TNT premiered “ High Value Target: The Hunt for Saddam ,” a captivating dramatization inspired by my book about debriefing the captured former Iraqi president in 2003 and 2004. At the time, Saddam’s capture was the biggest event in the world and, to many in Washington, the hoped-for climax of the Iraq War. Many in Washington and Baghdad believed that with Saddam’s detention, things would soon settle down to normal. The U.S. would be able either to return home or to move on to other priorities in the Middle East.

I had studied Saddam’s career for several years prior to his capture, and I initially felt well-prepared for his interrogation. I noticed almost immediately Saddam’s enormous political skills and how he could be charming, affable, and, yes, even display a sense of humor if he felt his life as a prisoner would improve by doing so.

He could also be dismissive, irritable, rude, and condescending if he felt that our line of questioning, particularly about human rights abuses, was beneath his dignity to answer. As we began to get to know each other, I realized that there were many more facets to Saddam’s history than the black and white caricature that many Western experts believed to be true.

Now, did this mean we had misunderstood who Saddam was? Not at all. He was a ruthless and brutal dictator who used ruthless and brutal tactics against his enemies and own people. Perhaps his failing was his inability to understand how best to advance relations with Washington that would benefit both Iraq and the U.S. I think he understood that his invasion of Kuwait had been a grave mistake that put him in a weakened position in the region and with the U.S. for the rest of his time in power.

Looking back, I still don’t understand why our government thought his regime posed a significant threat to U.S. security. He had been contained. We came to know later that he did not have weapons of mass destruction stockpiles, was not actively pursuing such weapons, and did not possess the material to build a weapon of mass destruction. Previous efforts to build such weapons had gotten Hussein nothing but trouble from the international community. Still, for purposes of deterrence, he wanted his enemies to believe he still had them.

If there was a winner in our war against Saddam, it was Iran. Saddam was the greatest hedge against Iranian dominance of the region and, ironically, if his regime still controlled Iraq, I strongly believe we would not be at war with Tehran today.

As Iran lashes out at its Arab neighbors in the current conflict, I am reminded of a conversation I had with a young Emirati professional who asked me if it was true that I had met Saddam. When I said yes, she asked me what I thought of him. After telling her, I asked what she thought of him. This bright young woman told me that she and many of her generation deeply admired him because he was the only one who was brave enough to stand up for the Arabs.

I have drawn my conclusions from what I witnessed firsthand. But as that young Emirati woman reminded me, history can look very different depending on where you stand.

John Nixon was a senior leadership analyst with the CIA from 1998 to 2011 and author of “ Debriefing the president: The interrogation of Saddam Hussein .” “High Value Target: The Hunt for Saddam,” a limited series based on his book that originally debuted on TNT , will be available to stream on HBO Max starting Oct. 14.

articles.title: 4 takeaways from the pre-election raid on Omar’s home
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Agents search Ilhan Omar’s home ▪ Zelensky leads backlash to diesel deal ▪ Judge slams DOJ over tree cutting ▪ Iran likely responsible for air base incident Federal agents searched the Washington-area home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) before dawn Monday in a major escalation of the Trump administration’s probe of…
articles.body:
▪ Zelensky leads backlash to diesel deal

▪ Iran likely responsible for air base incident

Federal agents searched the Washington-area home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) before dawn Monday in a major escalation of the Trump administration’s probe of a political adversary just three weeks before the midterm elections.

The search was carried out by agents with Homeland Security Investigations, an elite criminal unit of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and provoked fierce backlash from Democrats. The incident also raised questions among some legal experts about the long-standing practice at the Department of Justice (DOJ) of avoiding politically sensitive actions within 60 days of an election.

Here are some takeaways from the raid and its fallout.

Investigation centers on Omar’s immigration history

The court-approved search of the congresswoman’s home comes after Department of Homeland Security officials said in recent months that they were investigating Omar over her family’s immigration paperwork, which was filed by her late father when she was a child.

Omar, a member of the “squad” of progressive House members on Capitol Hill, was born in Somalia and fled the civil war there when she was 8 years old. She spent four years in a Kenyan refugee camp before arriving to the U.S. in 1995 and becoming a U.S. citizen five years later at 17 years old.

“We feel … there may be more to this — the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told conservative pundit Benny Johnson last month. “ There’s no expiration to that. If we can prove it — that you shouldn’t have been here in the first place — we’ll deport you.”

The search warrant listed a number of potential crimes under investigation, including false statements and fraud in immigration paperwork, and a general conspiracy charge, The New York Times reported , citing a person familiar with the document.

Timing breaks with long-standing DOJ norms

The search took place just 22 days before the Nov. 3 midterms. Mary McCord , a former senior DOJ official, told Morning Report that the move is a departure from “long-standing internal guidance” that prohibits prosecutors from taking actions that could even be perceived to have the purpose of “affecting an election or giving an advantage or disadvantage to a candidate or party.”

“Although special circumstances could provide an exception to that general rule, I see no indication based on the current reporting that would warrant an exception,” McCord said.

Former federal prosecutor Barbara McQuade said there is much unknown about the case, but what is known is that a magistrate judge found probable cause to believe evidence of a crime would be found at Omar’s home, the legal standard for obtaining a search warrant.

Thomas Hogan , an assistant law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston, said when he was a federal prosecutor, argued the 60-day norm has eroded over time, pointing specifically to the FBI’s handling of investigations during the 2016 election involving Hillary Clinton and President Trump, as well as in the years since.

“These norms went out the door with the Trump/Clinton election,” he said. “ Leaks about the Steele dossier and Trump and then James Comey’ s remarks about Clinton’s emails were central to the election.”

The president has repeatedly targeted Omar since she was elected to Congress in 2018, specifically attacking her Somali background and questioning her patriotism.

He did so again Monday, calling the congresswoman “totally crooked” in his first remarks on the raid.

“Well, I understand they’re looking at her very carefully,” Trump told reporters before departing the White House for Ohio. “I’ve always found her to be totally crooked personally, but that has nothing to do with me.”

“I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ,” he continued. “I have nothing to do with it.”

Omar, one of the first two Muslim women elected to Congress, has also been a frequent target on the right for her progressivism and outspoken criticism of Israel.

Following Monday’s search, Omar issued a defiant statement, accusing the president of “political intimidation” and saying she “will not be silenced.”

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar wrote in a post on the social platform X. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”

Democrats were outraged Monday after news of the raid broke, accusing the Trump administration of weaponizing the government to go after political adversaries.

They are vowing to investigate the Omar raid and other similar cases should they win back control of the lower chamber in November, as they are expected to do.

“The American people deserve transparency, and we will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice,” the top three Democrats in the House — Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.), Minority Whip Katherine Clark (Mass.) and Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar (Calif.) — said in a joint statement Monday.

▪ CBS News : Supporters of Omar hold rally in Minneapolis

▪ The Hill : The Memo: Trump critics allege abuse of power

Trump repeatedly attacked Omar and the state of Minnesota during his visit to Ohio on Monday evening to stump for Sen. Jon Husted (R), who’s facing a competitive race against former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D). The president is set to travel to Alaska today to support Sen. Dan Sullivan (R).

Pennsylvania officials confirmed the state’s sixth death connected to a case of measles, adding to the outbreak that’s become the worst the U.S. has seen in decades. More than 4,000 cases have been confirmed nationwide, including more than 1,000 in Pennsylvania.

Pope Leo XIV is being admitted to a hospital in Rome today to have a nodule on his lung removed , having revealed its existence earlier this week in a rare act of transparency from the pontiff. The surgery will require a weeklong stay in the hospital.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky speaks to the media after a German-Ukrainian business forum in Kyiv, Ukraine, Oct. 4, 2026. (Dan Bashakov, Associated Press)

DIESEL DISSENT : Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky , backed by his country’s European allies, is pushing back hard on Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, denouncing the U.S. president as “weak” for making the agreement.

Zelensky rejected Trump’s repeated insistence that the Russia-Ukraine war is to blame for the high cost of diesel fuel, telling Fox News’s Bill Hemmer on Monday that the Iran war is the cause.

“Everybody understands that it depends on the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.

Tensions over Trump’s deal have upset what’s been a decently stable relationship between the two leaders in recent months. Zelensky’s comments prompted Trump to repeat his call for Ukraine to hold elections.

Zelensky, who has long argued it’s impossible to hold an election amid Russian attacks, called for a 60-day full ceasefire to allow the country to hold elections. The Kremlin said it would stop for a day.

The Trump administration is also reportedly threatening to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Europe for Ukraine if Kyiv doesn’t stop its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.

Zelensky said Russia continued to hit Ukraine’s energy infrastructure Monday in violation of the energy ceasefire that Trump claimed over the weekend the two sides had agreed to.

Trump’s diesel deal has been met with similar pushback at home, with lawmakers from both parties saying it would help Russia as it continues its aggression against Ukraine and that it may be illegal under U.S. law.

▪ The Hill : Trump picks fight with GOP over Russia diesel deal.

▪ The Hill : Oil analyst skeptical diesel deal will lower prices.

FEDERAL REPRIMAND : A federal judge tore into the DOJ on Monday for the administration’s failure to provide sufficient notice before cutting down hundreds of trees in East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C., over the weekend.

The park is home to three golf courses, including an 18-hole public facility that offers affordable rates and serves tens of thousands of players each week. Trump has been pushing to convert the property, which is operated by a local nonprofit called the National Links Trust, into a championship-caliber course that can host professional tournaments.

The DC Preservation League and two individuals have brought a lawsuit trying to prevent the overhaul of the public golf courses.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued an order Monday blocking the National Park Service from conducting any further work on the site until at least 2 p.m. Tuesday as she considers whether to issue a longer block.

“I trusted you all not to do precisely what you have done,” Reyes said, yelling at the lawyers representing the DOJ, The Hill’s Zach Schonfeld reports .

She said the government has lost “all of its credibility” in the case.

▪ The Hill : Trump pushing to turn Florida golf course into presidential retreat.

ALL IN : Big Tech leader Elon Musk has given $276 million to Republican PACs and other organizations over the past three months, providing a major cash infusion as Election Day is fast approaching.

A spokesperson for Musk’s America PAC confirmed the amounts, which were first reported by The New York Times, to The Hill’s Miranda Nazzaro and Julia Shapero .

Musk gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for the Senate GOP, and $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for House Republicans.

Musk had previously suggested he might take a step back compared to his involvement in the 2024 race. The Times reported that Musk’s donations make him the largest known donor of the 2026 cycle.

The news comes as Musk and Trump have apparently moved on from a public feud, with the president awarding the billionaire the National Medal of Science last week.

▪ The Associated Press : ‘Musk’ documentary goes nationwide this week.

The president will travel to Wasilla, Alaska, where he will deliver remarks at 7:30 p.m. EDT. He will then leave to travel to Las Vegas, where he will spend the night.

The Senate will meet at 3:30 p.m. for a pro forma session.

U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle speak during a dedication ceremony at the chancery of the U.S. Embassy, Oct. 7, 2026, in Athens, Greece. (Mark Schiefelbein, Associated Press pool)

TROUBLE IN TRUMP WORLD : A pair of scandals concerning administration figures close to Trump are taking center stage as Democrats seek to tie Republicans broadly to an unpopular president in the midterms.

Trump confirmed Monday he’s considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle following The Wall Street Journal report that she asked a GOP donor to pay off her $100,000 credit card bill via wire transfer to avoid a paper trail as she was seeking Senate confirmation.

“Well, we’re looking at it. Yeah, we’re not happy,” Trump said, in response to a question from The Hill’s Julia Manchester .

The Associated Press previously reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were both frustrated with Guilfoyle and considering her ouster. The Journal has also reported new allegations that wealthy Greek businessmen helped fund Guilfoyle’s luxury travel.

Meanwhile, Trump’s longtime campaign advisers Chris LaCivita and James Blair have found themselves in controversy over work they did for a pro-Russian party in Republika Srpska, an autonomous region of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Trump said he would terminate them from their roles if their work conflicted with the White House.

Democrats believe the scandals have helped them paint Republicans as out of touch with a midterm election coming up focused on affordability, Manchester reports.

“People also are not stupid,” said one Democratic strategist. “When they’re struggling, they’re looking at who is gaining, right?”

Police guard a road leading to RAF Fairford, in Fairford, England, Sept. 28, 2026. (Alastair Grant, Associated Press)

FINGER POINTED : United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he’s all but certain that a suspected plot to attack a U.S.-operated air base in his country was directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), despite Tehran’s denials of involvement.

“I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard,” Burnham told British lawmakers Monday. “We will not tolerate these threats on our soil.”

In response to its conclusion, the U.K. summoned the Iranian ambassador and added two Iranians, including the head of the IRGC’s counterespionage operations, to its sanctions list. The ambassador repeated that Iran wasn’t involved and pushed for the U.K. to provide evidence for its claims, though Iran has previously said it considered the base to be a legitimate target.

Officials said the two Iranians were involved in conducting espionage and attacks on Iran’s behalf in Europe and the U.S.

Burnham previously said investigators had strong indications linking Iran to the incident, which happened outside the Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford air base last month.

A total of seven men — six British nationals and one dual U.K.-Iranian citizen — have been arrested in connection with the alleged plot. Officers evacuated the area around the base after men in vans deemed suspicious were seen outside.

Police said they found gasoline in three vans linked to the initial five suspects detained but no explosives.

The Hill’s Ellen Mitchell reports on how the plot and abrupt subsequent withdrawal of all U.S. bombers from the base are expanding fears about Iran’s capabilities to strike targets outside the Middle East. articles.title: Attorneys warned of difficulty accessing Christa Pike’s veins: Report
articles.summary: Christa Pike regained consciousness and was speaking days after receiving two doses of execution drugs.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Christa Pike’s former lawyer says her legal team had warned of problems accessing her veins prior to her botched execution in Tennessee, according to multiple reports.

“Well, I can’t say I’m surprised,” James Crowson, who previously represented Pike, told The Guardian . “I knew that there were a number of defense filings saying that she had compromised veins, and that was going to be a difficult and perhaps cruel procedure for her because it was going to put her at risk for exactly what happened.”

Last week, Pike, 50, regained consciousness and was speaking days after receiving two doses of execution drugs.

Her attorneys called her recovery “medically unprecedented” after she was placed on a ventilator following the bungled Sept. 30 attempt to make her the first woman put to death in Tennessee in 200 years. On Wednesday, they said the inmate was confused, “speaking limitedly,” and could not move her arms, one of which had a blood clot.

Pike, who was convicted in the 1995 torture and killing of classmate Colleen Slemmer, is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution, according to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPIC). Many details of the execution process remain secretive, and Tennessee officials say they are investigating what went wrong.

Previous Tennessee execution warning signs

Tennessee’s executioners had difficulties earlier this year with IV lines for another execution, leading to it being called off.

In May, state officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, after his executioners tried and failed for over an hour to establish an intravenous line. Gov. Bill Lee (R) announced soon afterward that the state would not try again for at least a year.

Since 2009, six other prisoners in three states — Alabama, Idaho and Ohio — have had executions halted because of difficulties establishing an IV, according to the DPIC.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: AI is making work faster, but creation of better jobs won’t be automatic
articles.summary: Finishing a task faster creates an opportunity. Whether that opportunity becomes more rewarding work, a chance to learn or simply another assignment depends on the decisions employers make.
articles.body:
Counting the jobs that artificial intelligence creates or eliminates will tell us only part of its economic impact. Just as important is what happens inside those jobs: whether employees spend less time on tedious tasks, develop new skills or gain opportunities to advance. Helping people work faster is valuable, but it is not the same as making their jobs better.

Among U.S. employees who have used AI in their jobs at least a few times in the past year, 63 percent say it helps them complete tasks faster. That is according to new findings from the American Job Quality Study — a partnership between Jobs for the Future, The Families and Workers Fund and Gallup. Forty-six percent said AI helps them produce higher-quality work, and 47 percent said it allows them to spend more time on the most interesting parts of their jobs.

Finishing a task faster creates an opportunity. Whether that opportunity becomes more rewarding work, a chance to learn or simply another assignment depends on the decisions employers make.

The benefits also start from an uneven distribution of use . Forty percent of college graduates use AI at least weekly, compared with 17 percent of employees without a college degree. Managers are more likely to use it regularly than individual contributors. And 52 percent of regular users hold jobs meeting the study’s multidimensional job-quality criteria, compared with 32 percent of employees who never use AI.

That does not mean AI created those better jobs. The same groups that tend to hold quality jobs — including more educated employees and managers — also tend to use AI. AI use is also highly concentrated among remote workers, according to my work . We should not mistake an advantage among users for evidence that handing everyone a chatbot will close the gap.

Nor should we conclude that workers without degrees have little to gain. Among employees already using AI, reported improvements in creativity and work quality are similar across education groups . College graduates are more likely to report working faster, but the educational divide in adoption does not appear across every reported benefit. That is a reason to broaden opportunities to use AI effectively, rather than reserve them for employees already considered technologically sophisticated and familiar with digital technologies.

Many of these differences reflect the work itself . Not every job provides regular access to digital devices or obvious opportunities to use AI directly. A wise response should recognize those differences, rather than treating identical adoption rates across occupations as the goal.

The question, then, is not simply how widely AI is used, but whether it helps businesses produce more — and whether employees share in those gains.

In a working paper I co-authored with Bureau of Economic Analysis economists Tina Highfill and Jon Samuels, we found that industries within states with higher worker-reported AI use in 2025 and 2026 had experienced stronger output growth since 2020. The positive relationship is clearer for output than it is for employment, where the estimates are less precise but still present.

But what remains is what happens inside workplaces: How can organizations redesign work so that both businesses and employees benefit from AI?

Another study I conducted , following more than 30,000 employees through the Gallup Workforce Panel, finds that workers who report a clear organizational AI strategy are substantially more likely to use AI frequently, even after accounting for demographics and other workplace perceptions. Among frequent users, greater trust in leadership is also associated with larger self-reported productivity gains. The evidence points toward communication and trust as complements to the technology, not optional additions after the software is installed.

Thirty-one percent of AI users say their use has led their employer to ask them to take on more responsibilities. That need not be a bad thing: Increased responsibility can open paths to advancement. But it can also mean more work without greater authority or compensation.

Meanwhile, 52 percent of all employees say they have less influence over the adoption of new technology than they would like. Employers should take that seriously. Consulting workers before changing their tasks is a practical way to identify what deserves automation, where human judgment remains necessary and what support employees need.

Employers should begin with paid time to learn and test approved tools on actual job tasks. Managers should explain which uses are permitted, how outputs will be checked, how responsibilities may change, and inspire deliberate experimentation. Training should reach frontline workers, not just the people who volunteer for an AI pilot. Employees should also be able to flag errors or question a proposed use without being labeled resistant to innovation.

Workers are already reporting time savings from AI, but turning those savings into better jobs requires decisions about what employees do next, what they have the opportunity to learn and how their contributions are rewarded. That is the part of AI adoption that employers cannot leave to the software. It must remain a human-driven exercise.

Christos A. Makridis is an associate research professor at Arizona State University and a senior researcher at Gallup.

articles.title: Trump 'looking at' firing ambassador to Greece: 'We're not happy'
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says he's "looking at" firing Kimberly Guilfoyle as U.S. ambassador to Greece amid allegations of improper conduct.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is "looking at" firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after mounting reports alleging improper conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. "Well, we’re looking at it," Trump told reporters at the White House before leaving for an Ohio campaign rally Monday afternoon. "Yeah, we’re not happy." Trump’s comments came after a senior U.S. official said Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were "extremely pissed off" by reports about Guilfoyle’s conduct and expected to make a decision on her future this week. TRUMP AND RUBIO WEIGH FIRING KIMBERLY GUILFOYLE AS MISCONDUCT AND DONOR BAILOUT ALLEGATIONS MOUNT The Wall Street Journal has reported a series of allegations involving Guilfoyle, including that she asked a Trump donor to pay a $100,000 credit card bill before her confirmation hearing while allegedly promising access to administration officials. The Journal also reported claims that Guilfoyle made a threat involving the Greek government, promoted the interests of a Greek construction and energy company, allowed a lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings and accepted improper gifts or services. Rubio, who was in Greece last week, was frustrated by reporters repeatedly asking him to address the allegations publicly. RUBIO SOUNDS CAMPAIGN-READY AS HE RAILS AGAINST OPEN BORDERS, GLOBALISM IN SPEECH FROM ANCIENT GREEK RUINS "You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something, and you reported it, it’s the gospel," Rubio told reporters Thursday at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart Greece, looked on. "It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things." BIDEN-ERA DIRECTIVE FOR DIPLOMATS TO PEDDLE DEI ON FOREIGN GOVERNMENTS SCRAPPED BY STATE DEPARTMENT A day earlier, Rubio said he would not discuss the allegations while visiting a foreign country, but defended the embassy’s work. "Suffice it to say our embassy here is doing a great job," Rubio said at a joint news conference with the Greek foreign minister. "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here." TRUMP JR UNDER SCRUTINY FROM OWN PARTY OVER PUTIN-LINKED OLIGARCH'S LAVISH GIFT Vice President JD Vance also weighed in last week, saying he did not know the full details of the specific case but rejected the idea of selling access to government officials. "Of course, I don’t like anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official," Vance told reporters. "I assume you’re talking about a specific case, and I can’t say with confidence that the case you’re talking about is actually reflective of the way you’re describing it." HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing through her lawyers. In a statement released late Sunday, attorneys David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall said the money she sought from the Trump donor was payment for public appearances and speaking engagements that predated her nomination. "Ambassador Guilfoyle has served, and will continue to serve, with integrity, honor and distinction," the lawyers said. "We are evaluating all available legal remedies to collect this debt and any other potential causes of action." The attorneys also denied impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying she "sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the department's travel regulations." BIDEN-ERA FBI TRACKED TRUMP FAMILY TRAVEL AND WILES’ CALLS WITH LAWYERS IN SECRET PROBE: DOCS A U.S. official told The Associated Press that the State Department's inspector general is looking into the allegations, though it was not clear whether a formal investigation had been opened. The State Department declined to comment to the AP on a potential inspector general probe. Top Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Senate Foreign Relations Committee and House Oversight Committee have called for an investigation into Guilfoyle. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Guilfoyle is a former California prosecutor who was once married to Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom and was engaged to Donald Trump Jr. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Conservative Indian Americans find anti-Indian signals in GOP’s moves
articles.summary: Indian Americans, especially young men, were part of the voting bloc that helped bring President Trump back to power in 2024. Now, a swirl of anti-Indian language among the online right has translated into moves from the Trump administration that seem to quietly target people of Indian descent living in the U.S. Some conservatives in…
articles.body:
Indian Americans, especially young men, were part of the voting bloc that helped bring President Trump back to power in 2024. Now, a swirl of anti-Indian language among the online right has translated into moves from the Trump administration that seem to quietly target people of Indian descent living in the U.S.

Some conservatives in that group are growing frustrated.

“Every Indian American conservative who I’ve talked to, who’s not right now within the halls of power, is basically angry about this,” said Anang Mittal, political commentator and former Republican leadership aide in the House and Senate. “There’s a sense of betrayal.”

A social media post from a Republican candidate for a state office in Texas brought the rhetoric to the forefront last month. Bo French, the nominee for Texas Railroad commissioner, posted a photo of students celebrating at a University of Texas (UT) football game with a racist caption about the ethnic makeup of the crowd.

“I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined,” French wrote.

Several further comments suggested or said that the students did not belong there because they are Indian.

Some Texas Republicans condemned the post, while French doubled down. The discourse spiraled into conservative infighting over whether the students — several of whom have since confirmed to the media that they are American citizens — represent an immigrant takeover of the country.

That tension reached a finer point last week. Vice President Vance announced Thursday the administration was suspending Microsoft and Adobe, along with several Indian tech services companies, from Permanent Labor Certification, a program that allows H1-B skilled worker visa holders to apply for legal permanent resident status.

Vance, during the press conference, said the companies took advantage of the visa program to bring foreign workers to the U.S. to work for lower pay than Americans. Microsoft has disputed this.

“For every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one-and-a-half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said.

The affected foreign workers are statistically likely to be Indian: Nearly two-thirds of H-1B visa workers whose applications were approved in 2023 came from India. In a statement after the H-1B press conference, the company wrote that it’ll be providing the administration with more information and pushed back on the idea that its visa applications were for new immigrants coming to work for Microsoft in the U.S.

Amid the swirl of online right-wing backlash against Indians living in the U.S., the move from Vance felt targeted to some.

“All these policies are coming in the light of the rhetoric, and so it does seem like it’s aimed at, you know, creating pain for a certain subset of society, and you can say, ‘Oh illegal, illegal,’ but like you guys seem to keep harping on about H-1Bs and Indians,” Mittal said. “Like what am I supposed to say?”

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott , when asked about French’s comments, said, “That is not my message,” and that the picture was an example of “a way Texans unite.” Then he added: “That doesn’t mean that Texas cannot also lead in having the toughest immigration laws of any state in America and freezing H-1B visas at our universities.”

To Renu Mukherjee , visiting fellow at the Foundation for Research on Equal Opportunity, Abbott’s statement linking the two was revealing.

“Well, first of all, no one mentioned the H-1B visa, and second, like, it’s not even related to an employment visa, like we’re talking about 20-year-old undergrads at a UT football game,” Mukherjee said. “So I think there’s examples like that where the H-1B visa and discussion and criticism of it can sometimes, from certain elements of the right, be perceived as like this mask for anti-Indian rhetoric.”

The actual policy debate that arose from French’s post wasn’t about employing Indian workers on visas as much as about allowing Indian students in the American education system. Some right-wing voices protested that “families in Texas” were struggling to get their kids into college at UT because the university was accepting foreign students instead.

By state law, students who graduate in the top 5 percent of their high school class get automatic admission to public universities. A significant majority of UT students are admitted this way. And only around 9 percent of all students at UT Austin are international students.

But the conversation around the UT photo, Mukherjee said, exposed simmering hostility on the right toward Indian Americans’ success in higher ed, just as the move on Microsoft’s visas demonstrated that the Trump administration does not want Indian H-1B employees of Microsoft living in the U.S. to pursue legal status.

Republicans should be actively courting, not seemingly rejecting, the Indian American vote, she added. Instead, voters of Indian descent are now less likely to be interested in supporting a party that has embraced anti-Indian voices and ideas.

“10 months ago, I wrote that Indian Americans’ belief in merit, free markets, the American Dream, faith, family, the list goes on, made them a natural GOP constituency,” Mukherjee said in a post on social platform X last month. “All Republicans had to do was engage in some outreach and, of course, not be racist. Many (not all) failed.”

Welcome to The Movement , a weekly newsletter looking at the influences and debates on the right in Washington. I’m Helen Huiskes, Senate reporter.

Send me tips, comments, and suggestions: hhuiskes@thehill.com

PROPOSED CHANGES TO THE CENSUS WOULD REMOVE RACE CATEGORIES, BAR NONCITIZEN COUNTING

The administration is moving forward with a long-sought plan to reshape the census, eliminating racial categories and prohibiting counting of nonvoting citizens like immigrants in the country illegally, international students, asylum seekers, etc. The Heritage Foundation and other groups on the right have been pushing for these changes for years.

Proponents for these changes argue that racial categories separate people out by broad race banners that serve no purpose other than to justify Democratic gerrymandering.

“We’ve seen in other circumstances where the government does collect this racial data and uses this racial data, it has resulted in things that have been ruled unconstitutional that we view as deeply problematic, where you’re basically accumulating political power or apportioning political power based on demographic classes, and opposed to something like citizenship or other, more important angles of representation,” said Douglas Blair, spokesperson at Heritage Action, referring to the April Supreme Court decision that said Louisiana should not have drawn a new majority-Black House district.

But census data is not just about congressional districts — federal funding apportionment is often determined by population data. Planning decisions in communities about where to build things are informed by how many people live there and what they need.

Justin Gest , professor of law at George Mason University, wrote in a guest essay for The New York Times that the new census rules would fail to count nearly 16.5 million people and erase categories used in legal disputes over discrimination, as well as provision of federal resources.

“It’s difficult, for example, to prove that a business or other institution is discriminating on the basis of race without demographic base lines to measure against,” Gest wrote. “Remove the data, and you remove the grounds for many claims.”

Mike Gonzalez , a scholar at the Heritage Foundation who has advocated for these rule changes, wrote in 2024 that the census race categories exacerbate sociological sorting and allow liberals fodder for arguments about systemic racism.

“The racial data the census gathers is a faulty ground for policymaking. Successful Nigerian Americans over-identify as of Nigerian origin, for example, while successful Mexican Americans under-identify as of Mexican origin, skewing both populations in different directions,” Gonzalez said.

“Progressives will say that racial data collection helps to measure outcomes,” he added. “The Left insists that racial disparities are prima facie evidence of what it calls ‘systemic racism.’ But these categories are monolithic and arbitrary.”

The new proposed rules are expected to face legal challenges, as did Trump’s first-term effort to add a question on citizenship to the census, which the administration abandoned in 2020 amid a time crunch.

Read it here .

articles.title: Trump says he could be ‘last Republican president’
articles.summary: President Trump declared during a Monday political rally that he would “be the last Republican president” if Democrats clinch control of Congress and the White House in the next two elections. “I will be the last Republican president because they will add about 12 more electoral votes,” Trump said in his speech. “They’ll add four…
articles.body:
President Trump declared during a Monday political rally that he would “be the last Republican president” if Democrats clinch control of Congress and the White House in the next two elections.

“I will be the last Republican president because they will add about 12 more electoral votes,” Trump said in his speech.

“They’ll add four more senators. They’ll add 10 more congresspeople, approximately,” he continued. “They’re going to rig the Supreme Court through just a lot of people.”

The president added that Democrats want to raise the total number of justices on the high court to 23, adding 10 to the number that has been floated by party leaders.

“The real number that they dream of is 23,” Trump claimed during his speech. “They say 13. Who wants 13?”

Democrats have called for an “overhaul” of the court amid anger with Trump’s ability to appoint three conservative justices to the bench. Politicians such as former Vice President Kamala Harris have supported the idea of expanding the court to 13 justices along with Electoral College reform.

Trump was in Youngstown, Ohio , on Monday to stump for incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy (R), as both candidates are engaged in tight races in the Buckeye State despite the president’s victories there in the last three presidential elections.

While some GOP candidates this election cycle have sought to distance themselves from Trump and his plummeting job approval numbers , both Husted and Ramaswamy have relied on him to boost support among the Republican base.

“The Youngstown area for decades used to vote Democrat, and then you ran for office in 2016 and flipped it red forever,” Husted said during his speech Monday. “Is that right, folks?”

The president also endorsed several other Republican candidates who were present at the event, including Rep. Max Miller. The Ohio lawmaker has been accused of abusing his ex-wife and their young daughter — allegations he has denied.

“Thank you, Max, for coming,” Trump said. “Thank you. Very good.”

articles.title: Trump vanishes from GOP senator's campaign website as poll numbers plunge weeks before election
articles.summary: Sen. Mike Rounds' campaign scrubbed several Trump mentions from his website as the president's approval rating craters in South Dakota's Senate race.
articles.body: A Senate Republican running for re-election in ruby-red South Dakota has joined a growing number of candidates putting distance between themselves and President Donald Trump. But it’s more subtle than Republicans opposing the Iran war or dodging Trump campaign visits as Election Day nears and his popularity struggles. Just last month, Trump’s name and endorsement were featured prominently on Republican South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds’ campaign website, but some mentions of the president have since been scrubbed, according to an older version of the website reviewed by Fox News Digital. SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS Rounds’ campaign noted to Fox News Digital that not every mention of Trump has been removed. "The president’s endorsement is still front and center on the website in Mike’s announcement video," Rounds’ campaign advisor, Rob Skjonsberg, told Fox News Digital. "But, generally speaking, it’s not abnormal to hone in on general election messaging." Trump endorsed Rounds last year and lauded the lawmaker as an "incredibly strong advocate for the wonderful people of South Dakota, a State I love, and WON BIG, in 2016, 2020, and 2024!" "Mike Rounds has my Complete and Total Endorsement for Re-Election — HE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN," Trump said on Truth Social at the time. Still, Trump’s approval rating among voters has cratered — a Fox News poll last month found that overall, voters had a 39% approval rating of the president’s performance. Key issues like cost of living, cost of groceries and fuel, and the ongoing war in Iran were major sticking points for participants. FOX NEWS POLL: MOST RATE THE ECONOMY NEGATIVELY, INCLUDING HALF OF REPUBLICANS Rounds’ campaign website featured two mentions of Trump on its homepage, including "Endorsed by President Trump" and a photo of Rounds touting that "Mike is endorsed by President Trump and is working for South Dakota every single day." Those two mentions have since been removed, along with Trump’s name being removed in two places from the lawmaker's "Issues" page on his website — the president was previously included in Rounds’ "Put America First" and "Education" sections. The lawmaker is vying for a third term in deep-red South Dakota, where he previously served as the state’s governor and in the state Senate. He’s running against independent Brian Bengs, who previously ran as a Democrat against Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., in 2022. Thune easily defeated Bengs in the general election, securing over 70% of the vote. I hope Mike finds the courage to debate me, so we can talk about it." And South Dakota, unlike other red states like Kansas, hasn’t budged from being considered "Solidly Republican," according to the Cook Political Report. Other Republican candidates in tighter races, like Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa and former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan, have publicly come out against some of Trump’s policies, including the war and embrace of data centers. We’re proud of the president’s endorsement. It’s still front and center," he continued. "And, Bengs still wants to increase your taxes, take away your guns and expand Obamacare."

articles.title: The Supreme Court has a shadow docket — it needs a shadow court
articles.summary: It would present a disciplined mechanism for shadowing the issues that come before the court of last resort.
articles.body:
In England and other parliamentary countries, the loyal opposition appoints a shadow cabinet from among its members. A shadow cabinet has no formal legal power. Each shadow minister has specialized knowledge to critique policy in areas like defense, foreign affairs and finance.

If worthy of its shadow, the opposition creates an alternative agenda, as though a government is waiting, elaborating on the platform that could turn up in the next election cycle and bring the shadow government into power.

I discussed the possibility of a shadow cabinet in the United States with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), to counter the horrors of a Defense secretary like Pete Hegseth or a Health and Human Services secretary like Robert F. Kennedy Jr. She said she had presented the idea to minority leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), but he had no appetite for it.

So, let’s try another institutional framework. How about a shadow court to ride shotgun on our supremely partisan Supreme Court?

Suppose we had another constitutional court, selected more democratically, instead of having people appointed by a president who may or may not have been popularly elected and confirmed by a malapportioned Senate, where Wyoming has the same representation as California with roughly 1/67th of its population .

A shadow court — with House, not Senate confirmation, and term limits instead of lifetime tenure — could take on the same issues, maybe even the same cases as the Supreme Court. A thought-provoking book published last month, “ The Shadow Court: Rescuing Democracy from the Supreme Court ” by Fordham law Professor Julie Suk proposes just that. Suk suggests that “shadow justices could freely develop persuasive lines of constitutional reasoning with the political branches and the people as their audience.”

The Supreme Court has unbridled power to make policy from sources outside the Constitution.

There is no explanation for Bush v. Gore — which gave George W. Bush the presidency despite Al Gore winning the popular vote — other than five justices didn’t like Gore. There is no explanation for Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization other than five justices didn’t like abortion. There is no explanation for Trump v. United States other than six Republican justices did not like to see Trump prosecuted as a former president for criminal acts committed while in office. The term qualified immunity appears nowhere in the Constitution.

We needn’t mention Citizens United , which opened the floodgates to dark money in politics, or Trump v. Slaughter , which allowed Trump the power to politicize the independent administrative agencies. And I could go on.

The Supreme Court has vast power and minimum accountability. As Justice Robert Jackson put it , “We are not final because we are infallible, but we are infallible only because we are final.”

At no point does the Constitution’s text confer the power to set aside federal statutes. Chief Justice John Marshall seized that power in 1803, declaring “It is emphatically the duty of the Judicial Department to say what the law is.” Our Supreme Court is inefficient in discharging that duty. It cannot say what the law is in the abstract. It can only decide “ cases or controversies ” where the plaintiff shows real injury. In many countries, there are constitutional courts which largely arose in the 20th century that can address constitutional questions in the abstract. Not so in America.

Many foreign systems permit advisory opinions at various stages of the legislative process. In those jurisdictions, specific parties, usually including the legislative minority, can request an advisory opinion before or immediately after the passage of a law.

Today, the federal government can’t undertake any important action if five members of the Supreme Court don’t think it’s a good idea. And once that majority has spoken, that’s all she wrote.

By nominating shadow justices and appointing them through House confirmation, we would have a far more democratic process than we have now. Congress by statute could require the selection to be made from a list provided by “ a democratically accountable body .” It could require shadow justices to be lawyers with demonstrated qualifications in constitutional law and litigation.

“An additional court that is composed more democratically will make constitutional law more legitimately,” wrote Suk.

Any such change might face hostility from the present court, which may retreat turtle-like into a shell of self-protectiveness. But a conservative majority striking down a shadow court authorized by Congress would be an unseemly stretch.

Would the shadow court be any more influential than a law review article or an amicus brief? Maybe not. But it would present a disciplined mechanism for shadowing the issues that come before the court of last resort. The Constitution itself has authority only because it is persuasive. Constitutional law is a sustained argument about the meaning of democratic self-government. A body that offers a reasoned critique of the current court might, over time, enrich this dialogue and compel moderation.

We have a shadow docket where the court makes snap judgments; all too often decided without sufficient briefing, oral arguments or signed opinions explaining the court’s reasoning. Why not a democratically-appointed shadow court?

After all, the Constitution itself begins with the words, “We, the People.”

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst .

articles.title: Trump mocks heckler punched at Ohio rally
articles.summary: President Trump ridiculed a woman who protested his speech Monday at a political rally in Youngstown, Ohio, after the heckler was physically assaulted by a crowd member. The woman, who was wearing a “Release the Epstein Files” shirt, was punched in the face by a crowd member at the event while rallygoers cheered on the…
articles.body:
President Trump ridiculed a woman who protested his speech Monday at a political rally in Youngstown, Ohio, after the heckler was physically assaulted by a crowd member.

The woman, who was wearing a “Release the Epstein Files” shirt, was punched in the face by a crowd member at the event while rallygoers cheered on the assault with chants of “USA.”

Police later intervened and removed her from the venue, while the man who punched her remained inside and exchanged high-fives with other attendees, according to Fox News .

Trump, who had been criticizing Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown (D) before the altercation broke out, suggested the heckler was a “paid protester.”

“They’re all paid,” the president said. “They get paid by the lefties in order to destroy our country. They’re scum. But he’s going back home to mom.”

He also mocked the woman as she was being pulled out of the venue by police, calling her a “fat guy” and saying she “needs to go on a diet.”

During a rally in San Antonio on Wednesday, several protesters were escorted out of the event after disrupting the president’s speech. One crowd member pulled the hair of a man who heckled Trump while the crowd chanted “USA.”

“If there are any more paid protesters, please raise your hand and get the hell out of here,” Trump said at the Texas event.

The president has faced mounting backlash over his administration’s handling of the release of documents related to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and ri s ing costs amid the ongoing Iran war .

Several Republican candidates running in battleground states this election cycle have attempted to distance themselves from the Trump brand as the commander in chief faces sinking approval ratings ahead of the November elections.
