articles.title: Office mandates don’t just change where we work — they change how we think
articles.summary: America’s work culture has always rewarded the person who takes initiative, challenges assumptions and ships something new.
articles.body:
The train platform fills before sunrise as commuters funnel toward the same downtown blocks, coffee cups in one hand and laptops in the other. Inside the cars, the workday has already started, with earbuds in and Slack open.

Across the globe, another workforce starts the same morning with a quieter ritual: a focused hour at a kitchen table, a school drop-off, then deep work before the first meeting of the day. That pattern shows up clearly in work-from-home share estimates and in Federal Reserve Economic Data tracking paid days from home.

A recent cross-country analysis in the prestigious Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences puts culture at the center of the remote-work map. Using the Global Survey of Working Arrangements across 37 countries, the authors report that cultural individualism explains 29 percent of the variation in work-from-home rates across countries, a larger share than job structure, density or income. The study also reports a strong positive correlation between national individualism and average days worked from home, with North America and northern Europe at the top and East Asian countries at the bottom.

That relationship makes intuitive sense in a country built on personal latitude. In relevant measures, the United States sits near the top, with an individualism score of 91 that signals a preference for autonomy and self-direction. Remote work operationalizes that value at scale — it shifts time and task execution away from constant visibility and toward output and self-management.

The American remote-work baseline also looks durable. In the U.S., full days from home settled around a quarter of paid workdays in recent harmonized estimates, and the FRED series shows the same post-pandemic plateau pattern in a public time series. Americans embraced flexible norms because the model matches how many professionals already want to work: independently, with wide discretion, and with accountability tied to results.

Return-to-office mandates do more than change where people sit — they change what organizations reward. A rigid mandate elevates compliance, face time and centralized control as signals of commitment. Those are collectivist-coded behaviors: stay close to the group, align quickly, defer to hierarchy, and reduce variance in how work gets done.

Research on mandates and labor flows gives leaders a clear warning. In an illuminating study , researchers use large-scale resume data to estimate causal effects of return-to-office mandates at major tech firms, finding workforce composition shifts that include losses concentrated among longer-tenured and more senior employees. Senior talent carries firm-specific context, mentoring capacity and the confidence to challenge weak ideas. When that group walks, innovation slows through sheer loss of judgment and initiative.

An office mandate also collides with revealed worker preferences. In alternative work arrangements evidence from a hiring experiment, many workers show meaningful willingness to trade pay for schedule and location flexibility. When leadership replaces flexibility with a blanket office rule, competitors gain a clean recruiting pitch: autonomy, trust and modern work design. The result looks like a cultural mismatch inside the firm, with employees adapting by becoming quieter, more cautious and more focused on rule-following than value creation.

That is the hidden cost of enforcing sameness. People learn fast what behavior “wins.” Under an office mandate, the safest move becomes consensus and visibility. The bold move becomes career risk.

Individualism carries an economic edge because it rewards original contribution. A long-run cross-country line of work links individualist norms to stronger innovation incentives, including status rewards for innovators, in the innovation advantage argument and the accompanying cultural growth framework. Those incentives show up inside firms as well: employees propose, test, and ship ideas faster when leaders grant real autonomy and evaluate outcomes.

Motivation science points the same direction. In workplace-focused syntheses of self-determination theory, researchers emphasize autonomy as a core driver of intrinsic motivation in the autonomy research literature. Creativity thrives when people feel ownership over their work and agency over how they deliver it. Remote and hybrid arrangements create that agency by default, especially when managers measure deliverables instead of attendance.

Remote work also connects to entrepreneurial spillovers. A recent research summary on employee transitions highlights how widespread work-from-home can shape moves from wage work into founding, a critical engine in the American economy. When large companies enforce rigid office policies, they push autonomy-seeking builders toward smaller firms or their own ventures, where control over time and craft comes standard.

Of course, remote work still requires deliberate design. Large-scale evidence from a collaboration network study shows how fully remote shifts can make internal networks more siloed. The practical implication favors intentional hybrid rhythms, strong onboarding and planned cross-team collisions, while keeping day-to-day autonomy intact. A blunt mandate trades those targeted fixes for a cultural reset toward control.

America’s work culture has always rewarded the person who takes initiative, challenges assumptions and ships something new. Remote work amplifies that impulse by giving people back control of attention and time. Companies that force a broad return to office steer their systems toward conformity and compliance, and they pay for it in talent flight, slower creativity and weaker entrepreneurial energy. The competitive path runs in the opposite direction: trust adults, measure outcomes and let individual drive power the next wave of growth.

Gleb Tsipursky, Ph.D., serves as the CEO of the future-of-work consultancy Disaster Avoidance Experts and wrote “ The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results ” and “ ChatGPT for Leaders and Content Creators .”

articles.title: Kacey Musgraves fires back after Noem jab over Talarico
articles.summary: Kacey Musgraves is hitting back at Kristi Noem after the former Homeland Security secretary took a music-related political dig at her. In a Monday post on social media, Noem voiced support for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Republican’s Senate bid against Democrat James Talarico. Noem knocked Musgraves after Talarico attended one of the…
articles.body:
Kacey Musgraves is hitting back at Kristi Noem after the former Homeland Security secretary took a music-related political dig at her.

In a Monday post on social media, Noem voiced support for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Republican’s Senate bid against Democrat James Talarico.

Noem knocked Musgraves after Talarico attended one of the “Dry Spell” singer’s concerts over the weekend and shared photos of himself smiling alongside the country music performer.

“I’ll take @ellalangleymsic over Kacey Musgraves any day,” Noem said, tagging singer Ella Langley, whose song “Choosin’ Texas” has dominated the music charts for months.

“And if I’m choosin’ Texas, I’ll take Ken Paxton over James Talarico,” the former South Dakota governor added.

In a post to her more than 950,000 followers on the social platform X, Musgraves on Monday shot back.

“I don’t think you have a dog in this fight,” Musgraves said, “but if you did you would have shot it.”

The jab appeared to reference an anecdote Noem detailed in her 2024 book, “No Going Back,” in which she said she once took her 14-month-old dog — a German wirehaired pointer named Cricket — to a gravel pit on her property and shot it.

Noem, who was fired as Homeland Security secretary by President Trump in March, later described the dog as “extremely dangerous.”

In addition to Musgraves’s canine-focused retort, the 27-year-old Langley also appeared to untag herself from Noem’s post.

articles.title: Harris, Vance leading in 2028 presidential polling
articles.summary: A new poll found former Vice President Kamala Harris and Vice President Vance leading among potential 2028 presidential candidates. The Focaldata/Financial Times poll found 30 percent of respondents chose Harris as the 2028 presidential Democratic nominee, while 38 percent picked Vance as the Republican nominee. In the Democratic primary, 15 percent of respondents supported California…
articles.body:
A new poll found former Vice President Kamala Harris and Vice President Vance leading among potential 2028 presidential candidates.

The Focaldata/Financial Times poll found 30 percent of respondents chose Harris as the 2028 presidential Democratic nominee, while 38 percent picked Vance as the Republican nominee.

In the Democratic primary, 15 percent of respondents supported California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), 9 percent chose Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), 9 percent went with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and 8 percent chose Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.).

On the GOP side, Secretary of State Marco Rubio netted 24 percent support from respondents, 9 percent picked Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), 7 percent chose Donald Trump Jr. and 7 percent picked Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Fourteen percent were unsure which candidate they would choose in the Democratic primary and 12 percent were unsure regarding the GOP primary.

Vance entered the presidential conversation when he picked up support from many in President Trump’s inner circle. Trump has also repeatedly egged on the competition between Vance and Rubio for the 2028 Republican nomination. Vance even jokingly likened the competition to the president’s former reality show, “The Apprentice.”

Rubio told donors and other allies that he will not run, particularly against Vance, sources told The Hill . The vice president told NBC News in October, however, that he was focused on the 2026 midterm elections, adding “that’s what I’m going to keep on doing.”

Harris — who lost to Trump in the 2024 presidential election — has reentered the presidential conversation amid her attendance at campaign events for candidates in battleground elections like Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

A longtime donor of Harris’s told The Hill earlier this year that “she’s a smart woman and also isn’t going to do something fruitless for no reason” if she decides that the support is not there.

Newsom said earlier this year he would not run for president in 2028 if Harris ran again, pointing out that they would both be fighting over the same supporters.

Ossoff, meanwhile, told WSB-TV in August he had “zero interest in running for president in 2028.” Ocasio-Cortez said she will make a choice on whether to make a presidential bid following the midterms.

The Focaldata/Financial Times poll was conducted among 2,553 U.S. adults from Oct. 2-5. The Hill has reached out to Focaldata for the poll’s margin of error.

articles.title: Salazar picks up Colombian president’s endorsement after breaking with Trump on immigration
articles.summary: Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) is touting an endorsement from Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, amid a tight reelection contest where she has broken with President Trump over his hard-line immigration policies. “I receive with immense pride the support of my friend, President Abelardo de la Espriella,” Salazar posted on the social platform X.…
articles.body:
Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) is touting an endorsement from Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, amid a tight reelection contest where she has broken with President Trump over his hard-line immigration policies.

“I receive with immense pride the support of my friend, President Abelardo de la Espriella,” Salazar posted on the social platform X . The congresswoman shared a video of de la Espriella describing her as Colombia’s best friend in the U.S. Congress.

“Representing thousands of Colombians in South Florida has made Colombia a cause I carry with me every day to Congress,” Salazar wrote in her post.

De la Espriella is a dual Colombian and U.S. citizen, and he owns property in Salazar’s district, NBC News reported . He and his wife have donated nearly $90,000 to Salazar in the past, according to the report.

De la Espriella is also a close ally to Trump, who endorsed the Colombian leader ahead of that country’s election in June. In August, the State Department announced it intends to pledge $1 billion in assistance for security.

De la Espriella’s endorsement comes after Salazar publicly criticized Trump’s immigration policy as betraying Hispanic voters. Trump did not retract his endorsement for her reelection but criticized her as weak on border security.

“I’m very strong on the borders, and she isn’t. And she’s a nice person. I got her elected. Without me, she wouldn’t have gotten elected,” Trump said, responding to reporters’ questions last month.

The Cook Political Report rates Salazar’s race for Florida’s 27th District as “competitive,” even as Salazar has a significant fundraising advantage over her Democratic competitor, Eliott Rodriguez.

Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, predicts Salazar has a 76 percent chance of holding on to her seat.

articles.title: Supreme Court to hear DOGE’s bid to avoid turning over internal documents
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday agreed to review a requirement that the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) turn over internal communications in ongoing litigation, which the Trump administration calls an “intrusive” demand that violates the separation of powers. The high court previously issued a ruling siding with the administration when it sought emergency relief. Now,…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday agreed to review a requirement that the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) turn over internal communications in ongoing litigation, which the Trump administration calls an “intrusive” demand that violates the separation of powers.

The high court previously issued a ruling siding with the administration when it sought emergency relief. Now, the dispute has returned to the justices on their regular docket.

Oral arguments are likely to be held early next year, with a decision expected by summer.

DOGE spearheaded job and funding cuts throughout the federal government in the early months of the second Trump term, sparking a wave of litigation from federal employees and grant recipients. Other groups filed lawsuits over DOGE personnel’s access to sensitive government systems. DOGE formally shut down operations on July 4, but many of its employees went to different agencies in technology or design roles.

At the center of the lawsuit is whether DOGE qualifies as an “agency” under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) statute. Trump formally created the group by issuing an executive action that renamed the existing U.S. Digital Service as the U.S. DOGE Service. In court, the Justice Department says it doesn’t qualify.

The case at hand began after Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), a left-leaning watchdog, sued DOGE to force it to answer FOIA requests.

To shed light on whether FOIA applies to DOGE, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper demanded the group disclose certain intra-executive branch communications about its work. Cooper is an appointee of former President Obama who serves on the federal trial bench in the nation’s capital.

The Supreme Court halted the order in June 2025, over the dissents of the liberal justices, saying the demand needed to at least be narrowed. In the latest round, Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in court filings that they only did so “slightly.”

“The lower courts’ approach also defeats FOIA’s objective of protecting the separation of powers,” Sauer wrote. “Subjecting advisory bodies to intrusive discovery triggers the very concerns that Congress sought to avoid.”

But CREW said the lower courts followed the justices’ instructions “to the letter” and dismissed any notion that they had completely foreclosed discovery in the case.

“That is not what this Court said,” the group’s attorneys wrote in court filings.

articles.title: Supreme Court to decide if Nigerian man’s cooking was ‘material support’ for terrorists
articles.summary: The Supreme Court agreed on Tuesday to take up a case involving a Nigerian man who was denied asylum in the U.S. after an immigration judge decided that he had provided “material support” for a known terrorist group by cooking for them despite being held captive at the time. The justices have granted the Justice…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court agreed on Tuesday to take up a case involving a Nigerian man who was denied asylum in the U.S. after an immigration judge decided that he had provided “material support” for a known terrorist group by cooking for them despite being held captive at the time.

The justices have granted the Justice Department’s request to review an appeals court ruling that found the forced labor was not a disqualifying factor under federal immigration law.

Oral arguments are poised for next year, with a ruling expected by the summer.

Izuchukwu Ozurumba was recruited in 2022 to work as a cook at a rural Nigeria camp about 12 years after he moved back to the country from Venezuela seeking better employment opportunities. He later learned the camp was run by the “Unknown Gunmen.”

Ozurumba was held in the camp for six months, where he was forced to cook meals for the group’s leaders, eventually without pay. He could not leave, as the camp was guarded by armed security.

He escaped while on a trip into town to buy groceries and became the target of repeated threats and harassment from group members who on one occasion “beat him with sticks and knives” following a church service in Lagos, according to court records.

Fearing for his life, Ozurumba fled to Venezuela. After five months, he traveled to the U.S. and surrendered himself to immigration authorities at the southern border in July 2023.

An immigration judge found he was removable from the country for entering without valid documents. Ozurumba filed for asylum, withholding of removal and protection under the Convention Against Torture, citing fear of returning to his home country.

An immigration judge denied Ozurumba relief and ordered in March 2024 that he be deported to Nigeria. The judge said he was not eligible for asylum due to an Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) provision known as the material-support bar.

The Board of Immigration Appeals affirmed that decision in September 2024, concluding the statute did not include an implied duress exemption.

A divided panel for the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals disagreed, finding that Oruzumba’s actions were not sufficient on their own to help the group accomplish its terroristic goals.

“Cooking meals using food and supplies purchased by the organization may have ‘sustained’ the organization in the broadest possible sense—by converting raw groceries into meals they enjoyed—but provided nothing that the organization could use or readily divert to plan or carry out its terrorist activities,” the appeals court wrote.

The appeals judges vacated the removal order and sent the case back to the lower court to review. But by that time, court records show that Ozurumba’s lawyers said he had already been sent back to Nigeria.

The appeals court declined at the time to order the federal government to facilitate his immediate return to the U.S. for further immigration proceedings.

articles.title: Supreme Court turns away Kari Lake lawyer’s challenge to sanctions in Arizona voting machine lawsuit
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to hear an appeal from a lawyer who was sanctioned while representing former GOP gubernatorial candidate Kari Lake in a 2022 lawsuit challenging Arizona’s use of electronic voting machines. The high court did not provide any explanation for its decision, leaving intact an appeals court ruling that upheld the…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to hear an appeal from a lawyer who was sanctioned while representing former GOP gubernatorial candidate Kari Lake in a 2022 lawsuit challenging Arizona’s use of electronic voting machines.

The high court did not provide any explanation for its decision, leaving intact an appeals court ruling that upheld the sanctions.

The lawsuit sought to force local election officials to use alternative methods to collect and count ballots for the 2022 midterms. It claimed that electronic systems used in Maricopa and Pima counties were unreliable and “vulnerable to attack and manipulation.”

The suit was filed that April, when Lake was running for governor and fellow Republican Mark Finchem was running for Arizona secretary of state. Both ultimately lost their elections.

A federal judge dismissed the suit in August 2022 for lack of standing. Lake’s legal team, including Andrew Parker and Kurt Olsen, was later ordered to pay $122,200 in sanctions after the judge found the claims were frivolous.

“Failing to impose meaningful sanctions here might very well encourage others to follow suit by lending their credibility to documents filed in court without facing any real consequence if their certifications prove hollow or incomplete,” U.S. District Judge John Tuchi wrote in his 2023 ruling. “The need for general deterrence is therefore significant.”

A divided panel for the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the sanctions in the spring of 2025.

Parker’s lawyer had urged the Supreme Court to reverse that decision, citing a dissent from six 9th Circuit judges who objected to the full court’s decision not to rehear the case and criticized Tuchi’s intent to “send a message” as an attempt to chill “politically disfavored litigation.”

“Permitting its sanctions decision in this case to stand will close the door to creative, aggressive, or novel claims and arguments for any client or lawyer unable to afford the cost of a sanctions order if the district court finds the arguments contrary to its own view of sound public policy,” attorney Nathan Lewin argued.

Olsen, who was sanctioned alongside Parker, was not listed as a party in the petition.

In response, attorneys for Maricopa County accused Parker of mischaracterizing the situation.

“Contrary to Petitioners’ claims, they were not sanctioned because they brought a long-shot, novel, or politically disfavored lawsuit,” they wrote. “Nor were they sanctioned because they challenged election procedures, or because they represented disfavored clients.”

“Petitioners were sanctioned because they made objectively false and misleading statements in documents that they signed and filed in a federal district court,” the attorneys added, also arguing Lake’s lawyers “unreasonably and vexatiously multiplied the proceedings” by ignoring warnings of potential frivolousness.

The Supreme Court previously rejected Lake and Finchem’s request to revive their lawsuit in 2024.

articles.title: Supreme Court to hear Trump attempt to withhold DOGE documents
articles.summary: The Supreme Court allowed a watchdog group to seek further information about the internal operations of the Trump administration’s Department of Government Efficiency that played a key role in firing thousands of federal workers and canceling various streams of government funding.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Tuesday took up the Trump administration’s bid to prevent a watchdog group from seeking information about the Department of Government Efficiency, which played a key role in firing thousands of federal workers and canceling government funding. The court agreed to hear a Justice Department appeal that sought to prevent Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington from obtaining records under the Freedom of Information Act. A ruling is due by the end of June. The Trump administration has argued that DOGE, spearheaded by former administration adviser Elon Musk, was not subject to what are known as FOIA requests. DOGE, which played a key role in dismantling the U.S. Agency for International Development, was a controversial feature of Trump’s early months in office, triggering various lawsuits. Its operations have since dwindled. The case had already reached the Supreme Court once at an earlier stage of the litigation. Then, in a provisional decision, the court blocked parts of a lower court ruling that required thousands of pages of information to be handed over. It also meant that plaintiffs’ lawyers could not depose Amy Gleason, the DOGE administrator. Litigation has since continued. As a result of the Supreme Court’s earlier intervention, the plaintiffs narrowed their requests for information, but the government still objected. After losing in lower courts, Solicitor General D. John Sauer again asked the justices to weigh in. The information requests remained on hold while the case plays out. The plaintiffs say the information they still want is about DOGE guidance to its workers on the canceling of contracts and firing of government workers. None of those requests concern any communications with the White House that may be off-limits under FOIA, they say. A key question lurking in the case is whether DOGE is technically a government agency and therefore subject to FOIA, which allows members of the public to seek internal documents. The Trump administration says that, despite its name, DOGE is merely a presidential advisory body that is not subject to public records requests under FOIA. Further complicating matters, when DOGE was set up, it effectively took the place of a previous government entity called the U.S. Digital Service. The Trump administration now refers to the body as the U.S. DOGE Service, or USDS. Soon after Trump took office in January 2025, CREW filed a FOIA request seeking information about DOGE. The group later filed suit. In March 2025, U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper in Washington ruled DOGE is “likely” covered by FOIA, saying that “the public would be irreparably harmed by an indefinite delay in unearthing the records CREW seeks.” The documents in question all relate back to the question of whether DOGE is a government agency.

articles.title: Supreme Court to weigh if Nigerian who cooked for terrorists can be denied asylum
articles.summary: The Supreme Court agreed to consider the Trump administration’s bid to deny asylum to a man officials say provided material support to terrorists in Nigeria by cooking food for them.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Tuesday agreed to consider the Trump administration’s bid to deny asylum to a man officials say provided material support to terrorists in Nigeria by cooking food for them. The case involving Izuchukwu Ozurumba focuses on a provision of immigration law that bars anyone from entering the U.S. if they have “engaged in terrorist activity,” which includes providing material support. The Trump administration has cracked down on asylum claims as part of its broader anti-immigration policy. Ozurumba claims he took the job working as a camp cook in 2022 before finding out that it was run by a separatist group called the Unknown Gunmen. He worked there for about six months, half of which was unpaid, before escaping, he said. Ozurumba sought asylum in the U.S. after crossing the southern border in July 2023, claiming members of the Unknown Gunmen had threatened to kill him. An immigration judge initially rejected his asylum claim, finding that Ozurumba had provided material support to the group by cooking three meals a day. Ozurumba was subsequently deported in April 2025, but his case continued, and five months later the Richmond, Virginia-based 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in his favor, saying that cooking did not qualify as material support. The justices will hear arguments and issue a ruling later in the court term, which runs until June. In the coming weeks, they will also decide whether to hear the Trump administration’s appeal seeking to maintain a broad block on asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border.

articles.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle, U.S. ambassador to Greece, resigns amid misconduct allegations
articles.summary: Guilfoyle, a former Fox News personality, was a top Trump campaign surrogate.
articles.body: U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle, once a top campaign surrogate for President Donald Trump, has resigned amid a misconduct probe. “Serving as the United States Ambassador to Greece has been the honor of a lifetime,” Guilfoyle said Tuesday in a post on X announcing her resignation. She also addressed “recent allegations against me, writing that “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.” Guilfoyle’s post came shortly after new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia told reporters that Guilfoyle had been asked to step down. “We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign,” Zacharia said at her inaugural White House press briefing. “She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well.” Speaking to reporters later Tuesday morning, Trump said of Guilfoyle that “She went to Greece. She was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading.” He added that he had not spoken to her. Guilfoyle, 57, the former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., has been under investigation by the State Department’s inspector general’s office, two people familiar with the decision confirmed to NBC News last week. The probe came after The Wall Street Journal reported allegations of misconduct in her role as ambassador, including allegations that she bragged about her connections to Greek tycoons who she said funded luxury trips for her. The article cited people who heard the conversation and an audio recording. NBC News has not independently confirmed the allegations. A Trump donor named Eric Deters came forward this month accusing her of asking him to pay her outstanding $100,000 American Express bill in the days before her 2025 Senate confirmation hearing in exchange for access to senior administration officials. “She was so desperate for that $100,000. It was a quid pro quo,” Deters told NBC News in an interview. “She said I could ask her for anything and everything in Trump world. There was no request too big,” he added. A text message provided by Deters appeared to show Guilfoyle instructing him to wire the money directly to American Express because “it won’t show up anywhere” that way. He said he did not pay her the money. Attorneys for Guilfoyle said in a statement Monday that Deters owed her the money for speaking engagements, which he denies. The attorneys, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also denied allegations of any impropriety involving her travel, saying she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations.” Asked Tuesday whether she was would launch her own investigation into Guilfoyle’s conduct, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, referred back to the State Department probe. “I think right now that there is an inspector general investigation in the Department of State. We’ll probably wait to see what comes, what happens with that,” Pirro told reporters. After the reports about her misconduct first surfaced last week, Guilfoyle thought she could save her job and was making calls to allies as recently as yesterday in a continued effort to do that, according to a source familiar with the matter. The person added that there was concern among senior White House aides about what a State Department inspector general probe would find and reveal that has not been made public yet and that could be embarrassing for the president and his administration. Asked Friday about the reports of Guilfoyle’s conduct, Trump said it was “too bad.” “I just heard a little bit about it. I don’t know too much, but she was always very nice,” he said. His tone had hardened by Monday. Asked whether he was considering firing her, he said: “We’re looking at it. We’re not happy.” Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended Guilfoyle last week. Vance said “these are accusations” and “we don’t try people in the court of public opinion.” “Let’s actually see what the facts are. Let’s see what the truth is, and obviously if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it,” he said. Rubio, meanwhile, ripped a reporter for asking about the allegations while he was with her in Athens. “We don’t conduct these things in a press conference on a tarmac in a foreign country because you wrote a story or somebody else wrote a story because some source gave it to you,” Rubio said Thursday. “I don’t even know if what you’re reporting is true.”

articles.title: Trump fires Kimberly Guilfoyle amid misconduct allegations
articles.summary: The White House said Guilfoyle had been asked to resign as U.S. ambassador to Greece after a series of reports on her alleged conduct in the role.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump is dismissing Kimberly Guilfoyle as U.S. ambassador to Greece after a series of reports raised questions about her conduct on the job.

The White House said Guilfoyle had been asked to resign after nearly a week of speculation that Guilfoyle, the former fiancée of Trump son Don. Jr., would be let go.

"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign. She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said during her first briefing with the media.

Trump campaign donor Eric Deters says Guilfoyle pushed him to pay off her $100,000 American Express bill while she was preparing for her Senate confirmation hearing last year. Guilfoyle is also said to have offered to make a businessman "a lot of f---ing money" during a conversation, in which she touted her connections to the Trump family earlier this year, the Wall Street Journal reported.

Both of the alleged incidents were reported by the Wall Street Journal, which said a lawyer for Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the messages she's said to have sent to Deters, a former congressional candidate.

Trump acknowledged on Oct. 12 that he was weighing whether to fire Guilfoyle, the ex-fiancée of his son Donald Trump Jr. , over potential ethics violations.

"Well, we're looking at it. Yeah, we're not happy," Trump told reporters, as he departed the White House for a campaign event.

Guilfoyle's fall from grace was a sharp turn of events for the former Fox News star who was once part of the Trump family's inner circle.

At a Greek Independence Day event at the White House on March 26, Trump embraced Guilfoyle and asked her to join him at the front of the East Room.

"Kimberly Guilfoyle has been my friend for a long time. I love calling her Kimberly. That's my little pet name, right? But you are the greatest, and I heard they love you over there. I hope you come back here in 12 years or whenever the term ends," Trump said at the time. "Come on up here, Kim, stay alongside of us."

Six months later, she was facing a congressional investigation over an allegation that she advocated for the U.S. to interfere in the democratic elections of NATO allies.

Democratic Rep. Gregory Meeks asked the State Department's Office of the Inspector General (OIG) to launch its own investigation and requested that Guilfoyle appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee and testify under oath.

The Justice Department could also end up investigating the allegation that Guilfoyle pushed a campaign donor to pay off her credit card bill, Washington, D.C., U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro indicated at an Oct. 13 press conference.

"I think right now that there is an inspector general investigation in the Department of State. We probably wait to see ... what happens with that," Pirro said.

At first, Guilfoyle seemed poised to potentially survive the allegations, with top Trump administration officials side-stepping questions about her conduct last week.

"Obviously, I don't love that," Vice President JD Vance told a reporter on Oct. 8 when asked about the idea of selling access to the Trump administration without using Guilfoyle's name or getting into the specifics.

He defended Guilfoyle to reporters the following day, saying the administration would follow the facts. "Let's see what the truth is. And obviously, if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences," Vance said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who happened to be in Athens at the time, said on Oct. 8 during a joint news conference: "The questions you're asking me, we're not addressing those at press conferences in Greece with the foreign minister and in another country."

He flashed anger later as a journalist asked him about the report again on the tarmac in Athens.

"I'm not going to comment on a story that literally posted a few hours ago," Rubio said. "I don't even know if it's true or not true. So it's just not going to work that way, and it most certainly is not going to work that way when I'm sitting in another country."

It was not immediately clear who Trump planned to tap to fill the role, which requires Senate confirmation. Greece is considered one of the more plumb ambassadorial positions as both a NATO nation and a member of the European Union.

The Senate confirmed Guilfoyle to the position in September 2025. The former media personality dated the president's eldest son for several years before a 2024 breakup that preceded Trump's return to office. She was previously married to California Gov. Gavin Newsom and served as first lady of San Francisco during the Democrat's mayoral term.

articles.body: The White House has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign as U.S. ambassador to Greece amid mounting allegations involving her financial dealings, treatment of embassy staff and relationships with foreign business interests. "We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign. She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," White House press secretary Katie Zacharia announced Tuesday during her first-ever briefing to the press. It is not clear whether Guilfoyle lodged her official resignation, and when asked for clarity, the White House referred Fox News Digital to the remarks from the briefing. The update from Zacharia came just one day after President Donald Trump publicly acknowledged that he was considering firing Guilfoyle, who was previously engaged to his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. Trump further distanced himself from the ambassador when asked about the reports and her status with the first family. "Kimberly Guilfoyle — she was almost a member of your family. How surprised were you to learn about these allegations? What did you think?," a reporter asked Tuesday before he left for Alaska. "She wasn't a member of my family. She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago," Trump said. "She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading." TRUMP 'LOOKING AT' FIRING AMBASSADOR TO GREECE: 'WE'RE NOT HAPPY' Guilfoyle was with Donald Trump Jr. for six years, four of which they were engaged. They publicly split in December 2024, the same month Trump nominated her to serve as ambassador to Greece. The ambassador came under scrutiny last week after The Wall Street Journal reported that she asked Trump donor Eric Deters to pay off a $100,000 American Express bill shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025. According to messages reviewed by the Journal, Guilfoyle urged Deters to wire the money directly to American Express, saying the transaction would not leave a paper trail, while offering to help him gain access to senior Trump administration officials. Deters said he never made the payment. Guilfoyle's attorney, Jesse Binnall, disputed the authenticity of the messages, saying Guilfoyle had been paid to speak at events before her nomination and "was owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events." The allegations followed an earlier Journal investigation into Guilfoyle's conduct in Greece, including claims that she promoted the interests of Greek construction and energy company Aktor Group and allowed its registered lobbyist, Christos Marafatsos, to accompany her to private diplomatic meetings with senior officials. The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle suggested at a dinner with Greek officials that the U.S. would undermine their government, citing political developments in Romania. Greece's foreign minister subsequently said there was no need to summon Guilfoyle for an explanation because the country's energy minister denied that any threat had been made. Separately, the State Department's Office of Inspector General reportedly opened an investigation into allegations involving Guilfoyle's treatment of embassy employees, private travel, acceptance of gifts and relationships with business interests, according to the Daily Mail. HOUSE DEMOCRAT INVESTIGATED OVER ALLEGED 'INAPPROPRIATE SEXUAL CONTACT' WITH STAFFER Sources described a hostile workplace in which Guilfoyle allegedly threatened to fire employees. They also claimed that she demoted members of her security detail over minor incidents, including an officer who reportedly failed to answer a 4 a.m. request for ice while she was vacationing in Mykonos. The inspector general's office declined to confirm or deny the existence of an investigation. Binnall told the Daily Mail that "any implication of wrongdoing by the Ambassador is unsupported." The allegations drew scrutiny from congressional Democrats, including Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., and Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., who called for a review of Guilfoyle's conduct. Let's see what the truth is," Vance told reporters in Ohio. "And obviously, if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it." Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who visited Greece last week and delivered remarks against the backdrop of the Acropolis, initially defended Guilfoyle's performance. "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here," Rubio told reporters Wednesday. A day later, Rubio declined to address the allegations directly, challenging reporters over their reliance on unnamed sources. "You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something, and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel," Rubio said last Thursday. Just days later, the White House announced their request for her resignation. Trump nominated Guilfoyle to the diplomatic post in December 2024. A former California prosecutor and longtime Trump ally, she previously served as a prominent surrogate and fundraiser for the president. articles.title: Trump’s new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia keeps first briefing short
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia held an unusually short first briefing with the media Tuesday, concluding after less than 15 minutes and calling on just three reporters, all from conservative outlets.
articles.body: President Donald Trump’s new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia held an unusually short first briefing with the media Tuesday, concluding after less than 15 minutes and calling on just three reporters, all from conservative outlets. The press secretary spent more than half of that time reading remarks before taking questions from Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail. In response to the Daily Mail, she also revealed that the administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, to resign following allegations of misconduct. Zacharia spent most of her remarks touting the president’s policies and framed her new position as a job to “amplify” the president, something she said she’d done as a conservative commentator. She referred to those appearances, telling reporters on Tuesday that she hopes to “take that into an official capacity.” Now, Zacharia said, she hopes to “only build on, only amplify, and only multiply, to the extent possible, all of the wins” that Trump is “making for Americans, for Americans to understand how much has changed in this brief period of time, what he’s been able to accomplish.” “My goal is to be able to communicate that in complete tandem with the president, as he is his own best spokesperson, and will absolutely be leading the way with that,” she added. Asked by Fox News whether the U.S. has stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, she said she would “have to get back to you on that.” Zacharia is stepping into the role as the top White House spokesperson in the final weeks before midterm elections, as the president is embarking on a series of campaign trips to shore up his base. She said Trump would continue his midterm “blitz,” pointing to future stops in Kentucky, Georgia and Florida. At the same time, voters are souring on the president’s performance, which Trump has chalked up to a public relations issue. Last month, an NBC News poll found that 41% of registered voters approved of the president’s performance, a second-term low. The same poll found that voters largely disapprove of the president’s handling of the economy. The administration hasn’t shown a path to ending the war in Iran, which has raised fuel prices and contributed to inflation. And in recent days, some Republican candidates in battleground races are breaking with the president on his handling of tariffs and the Iran war. Trump said during a recent rally in Oklahoma that the administration is “not doing a good job of public relations.” At a separate event, he said that the administration was “doing an extremely poor job of promotion,” despite doing an “extremely great job of running the country.” Zacharia painted a rosy picture of the president’s popularity, describing the Ohio venue of his rally on Monday as “overflowing with enthusiasm.” Attendance of the president’s rallies is at “record highs as enthusiastic, hardworking Americans are lining up and packing arenas to support President Trump and Republicans,” she said. NBC News has previously reported that the president has been speaking in smaller venues that are not filled. Zacharia also expressed her views on the shifting media landscape and discussed balancing her family life in response to other questions. She said she wanted to “expand” on the new media seat “to the extent possible,” referring to predecessor Karoline Leavitt’s decision to include a seat in the briefing room for non-traditional media. Breitbart held the seat on Tuesday. Leavitt said in August that she was departing the administration to spend more time with her family. Asked about balancing the job with her own family in California, Zacharia said her husband and four children are moving to the Washington area. “I adore my family. I love them. They are my priority,” she said. “I love being with my kids. The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable.” She then accidentally referred to her husband as “my president” before correcting herself and saying he would be in D.C. for the week. The president announced on Friday that he was tapping Zacharia to fill the position. She had served as a senior communications adviser for Trump Media & Technology Group. In a Fox News interview over the weekend, Zacharia said she was looking forward to “working for President Trump,” adding, “this job is not about me.” “This job is about him and how he wants to communicate to the American people,” she said on Saturday. Zacharia said that Trump showed her the ballroom site when she visited the White House on Friday. “Just to see this vision he has for building, but also for America and the greatness that America has and has always had and that he’s bringing back — I can’t wait to work for President Trump on Monday,” she said.

articles.body:
Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, resigned on Tuesday amid allegations of improper conduct while denying the claims and vowing to "vigorously defend" herself.

In a lengthy post on her personal X account on Tuesday morning, Guilfoyle thanked President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for "entrusting me with the extraordinary privilege of representing the greatest country in the history of the world."

Guilfoyle also denied the "recent allegations" against her.

"These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," Guilfoyle wrote. "I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."

Earlier Tuesday, Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary , announced during her first briefing that the administrstion had asked Guilfoyle to resign.

"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," Zacharia said when asked about the status of her employment in Athens. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well."

The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Guilfoyle asked a Trump donor to pay off a $100,000 American Express credit card bill ahead of her confirmation as ambassador in exchange for access to administration officials.

Guilfoyle, 57, was confirmed as U.S. ambassador to Greece in September 2025. According to the Journal, as Guilfoyle was preparing for her Senate confirmation hearings, she asked Eric Deters, a former Kentucky gubernatorial candidate and Trump donor, to send a $100,000 wire transfer to help pay down her American Express account "in a way that wouldn't leave a paper trail."

The report cited text messages between Guilfoyle and Deters.

"Honey please I need you to get this done for me today," she texted Deters, according to the Journal.

After the report was published, Deters told NBC News that he viewed Guilfoyle's request as a "quid pro quo."

"She was so desperate for that $100,000. It was a quid pro quo," Deters said. "She said I could ask her for anything and everything in Trump world. There was no request too big."

A lawyer for Guilfoyle initially told the Journal that she disputed the authenticity of the messages. In a statement released late Sunday, her attorneys denied that she had done anything wrong and said she was seeking payment for appearance fees that predated her ambassadorship.

On Monday, Trump told reporters that he was considering firing Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host who served as an adviser to his presidential campaign and was the fiancée of Donald Trump Jr.

"Well, we're looking at it," Trump said before leaving for an Ohio campaign rally. "Yeah, we're not happy."
